docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This project predicts the winner of an NFL game before kickoff. A user picks a home team and an away team in a web app, and the app shows a predicted winner and a win probability.

docs.title: What Is the Idea?
docs.text:
Teams that win more often, and outscore opponents by more, tend to win later games. The model compares the two teams on exactly two numbers, using only games already played earlier in the same season:

  • Win percentage difference: the home team's win percentage minus the away team's.
  • Point margin difference: the home team's average points scored minus points allowed per game, minus the away team's.

A logistic regression turns those two numbers into a home win probability. The numbers start over every season. The project does not use play-by-play data, injuries, weather, or betting lines. It is a small, complete example of a machine learning system, from data storage to a public web app.

The data is the nflverse game results file, limited to regular-season games from 2020 through week 10 of 2026.

docs.title: What Are the Phases and Steps?
docs.text:
Each phase ends with something that runs. Git commits and pull requests are done by the developer.

Phase 1: Data Pipeline (built)

  • Fetch the raw game file and save it unchanged.
  • Clean it: regular season only, 2020 to 2026 week 10, no ties.
  • Upload the cleaned table to a private S3 bucket.
  • Download it back from S3, so later steps start from the cloud copy.

Phase 2: Features, Training, and Tracking (built)

  • Build the two inputs and split games by season: train 2020 to 2024, validate 2025, test 2026.
  • Train the model and score it against the always-pick-home baseline.
  • Record every run in MLflow and save the trained model.

Phase 3: Local Prediction API (built)

  • Serve the model on your own computer with a FastAPI /predict route and a /health route.
  • Reject bad input with a clear error, and test with curl.

Phase 4: AWS Deployment (built)

  • Deploy the API to AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, with a public address.
  • Check that all 1,759 games get the same answers from the deployed model as from the local one.
  • See the implementation page for the steps and the Lambda package size, and Deployment Guide for the commands.

Remaining Phases (planned)

  • Phase 5: build the Vite web app and host it on S3 and CloudFront.
  • Phase 6: package the project in Docker.
  • Phase 7: write the README and finish the documentation.
  • Phase 8: review the finished project against the requirements.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The key decisions behind the project, in the order they were made. Each one states what was chosen, why, and what was turned down. The decision that shapes everything else, binary classification instead of regression, is explained in full first. Choices that still need the developer's approval are in Open Decisions.

docs.title: Why Binary Classification and Not Regression?
docs.text:
The choice: the model answers one yes-or-no question for each game: did the home team win? The answer is 1 (home win) or 0 (away win), stored in the column home_win. The model also gives the chance that the answer is 1. The alternative was regression, which predicts a number, such as the home team's point margin (home score minus away score).

Why classification fits this project

  • The question is who wins, not by how much. The web app shows a predicted winner and a win probability. A classifier produces both directly. A logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1, and the pick is that probability compared with 0.5.
  • A margin model needs an extra step to produce a probability. Regression would give an expected margin such as "home by 3.2 points". To show "58% chance the home team wins", that margin has to be converted using an assumption about how far real margins stray from the prediction. That assumption would have to be estimated and checked, and it is one more place to be wrong. The classifier avoids it.
  • Margins are noisy, and big margins are a poor guide to who wins. In the 1,759 games kept, the margin has an average of +1.56 and a standard deviation of 14.19 points, and ranges from -45 to +50. Games decided by 3 points or fewer are 429 (24.4%), and by 7 or fewer are 860 (48.9%). Games decided by 14 or more are 605 (34.4%). A regression fit on margins gives these blowouts a large pull on the fit, although a 35-point win says no more about who won than a 1-point win does.
  • The result is easy to judge. A classifier is scored by how often the pick is right, shown next to the rule "always pick the home team" (see the next section). A margin model is scored by an average error in points. Always predicting the average margin is off by 11.04 points on average, and a reader has no easy way to say whether 10 points of error is good.
  • It matches the data. A game ends with a winner or, rarely, a tie. The 6 tied games have no yes-or-no answer, so they are removed. This is covered in the Phase 1 Implementation.

What the choice gives up

  • The size of the win. A 1-point win and a 30-point win both count as 1 in the answer column. The model cannot say how close a game will be.
  • The margin is not ignored. It enters through the second input: each team's point margin per game in earlier weeks of the season. The model uses margin as evidence about team strength, and only the final answer is win or lose.

What was and was not tested

  • No regression model was trained or compared. The choice is made on design grounds above, not on a measured score. A regression comparison would also need a second set of scores and a conversion step, which this project does not build.

What would change the choice

  • If the web app needed to show an expected score or a point spread, regression (or a regression alongside the classifier) would be the right tool.

docs.title: Why Accuracy With a Baseline, and Log Loss as a Check?
docs.text:
• Accuracy is the headline score. It is the share of games where the pick matches the result.
  • It is always shown next to a baseline, the score of always picking the home team, which is the share of games the home team won (52.93% of the 1,759 kept games). A model only adds something if it beats that.
  • Log loss supports it. It scores the probabilities and not just the picks, so it checks that "70%" means about 7 wins in 10. The web app shows a probability, which accuracy alone cannot vouch for. It is reported for validation and test games only, because the model is fitted by pushing it down on the training games.
  • Reported whatever it is. The score is not tuned, and a poor score would still be stated.
  • Details: Phase 2 Part 2.

docs.title: The Data
docs.text:
• The nflverse games file, regular season only, 2020 through week 10 of 2026. That stays within the past decade and uses the most recent data. Week 10 of 2026 is the last week where every game has a score.
  • Ties are removed (6 games), rather than counted as an away win or half a win, because the question has exactly two answers.
  • The cleaned table goes to a private S3 bucket, and every later step downloads it back. Training always starts from the S3 copy, never from a local file, so every run uses the shared version of the data. The raw file stays on the developer machine.
  • The bucket is created by hand, not by code. A script that creates AWS resources adds risk for no benefit.
  • Details: Phase 1 Implementation.

docs.title: The Inputs and the Split
docs.text:
• Two raw per-game inputs, not ranks. They are the home team's win percentage minus the away team's, and the home team's point margin per game minus the away team's. Both use only earlier weeks of the same season, so a game's own result is never an input. A team with no games counts as 0.5 and 0.0, so week 1 gives 0 for both.
  • Why raw values. Ranks drop the size of a gap (a +14 team and a +2 team can be neighbors), create ties in early weeks, and change when unrelated teams win. Raw values keep the gap, need no tie rule, and read directly ("+7.3 points per game better").
  • The scores were similar, so the reason is clarity and not accuracy. Logistic regression with ranks got 169 of 271 validation games right (62.36%, log loss 0.6345) and 92 of 149 test games (61.74%). With raw inputs it got 171 of 271 (63.10%, log loss 0.6451) and 88 of 149 (59.06%).
  • Per game, not season totals, so a team that has played more games, for example after a bye, is not favored.
  • The split is by season, not at random. Training is 2020 to 2024 (1,339 games), validation is 2025 (271), and test is 2026 weeks 1 to 10 (149). A random split would put later games in training, and the model would be scored on games played before some of the games it learned from. The 2025 score is the one to report, and the test games never fit anything.
  • Details: Phase 2 Part 1.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
• Logistic regression only, with no model comparison. Turned down: a random forest as a second candidate, and XGBoost. One simple model is enough, the two inputs are simple, and an earlier test had the forest and logistic regression within a game or two of each other. Fixing the model type means the 2025 validation season is used only to report the score, so it is never used to choose between models.
  • A standardizing step is kept and saved with the model as one pipeline, so the API cannot skip it. The two inputs are on different scales: win percentage differences run from -1 to 1, and point margin differences run about -49 to 39.
  • Details: Phase 2 Part 2.

docs.title: Tracking and Reproducibility
docs.text:
• MLflow records every run, with its settings, scores, and files, so any run can be traced and compared.
  • The MLflow records stay local. mlflow.db, mlartifacts/, and models/ are not committed. The database is a binary file that changes on every run and records the artifact folder as a full path on one machine, and one command recreates all three with identical scores.
  • A small readable file, results/run-summary.json, is committed. It holds the settings, the data fingerprint, the scores, and the learned weights. It has no run ID, timestamp, git commit, or machine path, because each of those changes on every run and would show a change in git when nothing real changed.
  • The model is stored twice in each run, on purpose. The plain model.joblib is the working copy the API loads, and it carries the input names, version, and training seasons. The MLflow-format copy lets MLflow's own screen and loader open the model. MLflow's format alone was not enough: in MLflow 3 it is not in the run's file list, and it does not carry those facts.
  • Every run records the scikit-learn version and a fingerprint of the data file, so a run can be traced to the exact library and data it used.
  • Settings live in one file, config/config.yaml, and package versions are pinned. Changing a run means editing the file, not the code.
  • Details: Phase 2 Part 2 and Reproducing the Pipeline End to End.

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
• FastAPI, not Flask. The input checks (missing field, extra field, wrong type, out-of-range number) come from one request definition, and the test page at /docs needs no extra code. FastAPI also works with the Mangum adapter that Lambda needs. Flask would need a different adapter.
  • Strict input checks. Unknown fields, numbers written as text, NaN, and out-of-range values are rejected with status 422 and an error that names the problem.
  • The API uses NumPy, not pandas. The Lambda zip is 231.3 MB without pandas and 278.4 MB with it, against a 250 MB limit. See the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • The model loads once, at start-up, and the service refuses to start if the file is missing, unreadable, or built by a different scikit-learn version.
  • The pick rule is the scoring rule. A probability above 0.5 is a home win, and exactly 0.5 is an away win.
  • The API is built and tested locally first, with no Docker and no AWS.
  • Details: Phase 3 Implementation.

docs.title: Deployment and Front-End
docs.text:
Phase 4 (AWS) is built, with its brief and implementation page. Phases 5 and 6 are planned, in Remaining Phases.

  • AWS only: S3, Lambda behind an API Gateway HTTP API, and CloudFront, all in us-east-1, where the data bucket already is. Turned down: Google Cloud and Azure.
  • The same FastAPI app runs locally and in Lambda, using Mangum. Turned down: a separate hand-written Lambda function, which would repeat the input checks and the model call in a second place. See What Is Mangum?.
  • Lambda runs from a zip file. A container image in a private ECR repository is the fallback, used only if the zip goes over Lambda's size limit. The measured size fits.
  • Docker comes after the API, AWS, and the web app (Phase 6), with one Dockerfile and two targets, train and serve. Nothing before it needs an image. The README and the review (Phases 7 and 8) come after it, because they describe and check the finished project. Turned down: building Docker in Phase 3, which would put a packaging step ahead of the web app without unblocking anything.
  • The deployed model is checked on every game. All 1,759 games were sent through the public API and compared with the local model: every pick and every probability matched, and the accuracy from the deployed answers equals the run summary. The zip's hash equals the hash Lambda stores for the function, so Lambda runs the file built here. See Step 10.
  • Accuracy is the only priority for the deployment. Latency and cost are not concerns for this project. The Lambda function's memory is 1769 MB, and it may be changed if that helps, but it is not a priority.
  • CORS is set on the gateway only, with the CloudFront address and the local Vite address allowed. The CloudFront address is added once the distribution exists.
  • The API is public, with no key, no request limit, and no firewall for now. A key in a browser app would be visible to every visitor, so it would not protect the API. Protection can be added later if it is needed.
  • The front-end is a Vite app, and the published site is the built static files in a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront. Turned down: Streamlit, and S3's own website hosting (it serves only HTTP and needs a public bucket).
  • The web app reads one snapshot of the standings, taken after 2026 week 10.
  • The AWS deployment is a set of written steps, with no workflow file for it. Only the docs site is published by a workflow.

docs.title: Design Manifest
docs.text:
The initial project ideation was done with Gemini. The developer sets the requirements and constraints. The project is then built with spec-driven development: Kiro writes the spec, Cursor writes the code, Kiro adds the comments and docs, and the developer reviews and commits. Each piece of work starts as a written spec, and the code is built to that spec and checked against it. The docs are written from the finished code, so they describe what exists and not what was planned.

flowchart TB
    G["Gemini:<br/>initial ideation<br/>(once, at the start)"] --> A["Developer:<br/>sets requirements<br/>and constraints"]
    A --> B["Kiro:<br/>writes the spec"]
    B --> C["Cursor:<br/>implements the code"]
    C --> D["Kiro:<br/>reviews, adds<br/>comments and docs"]
    D --> E["Developer:<br/>reviews and commits"]
    E -->|"next task or phase"| A
  • Gemini produced the initial project ideation: the project idea and its starting scope, before any spec or code existed.
  • The developer sets the requirements and constraints. That covers the scope of each phase, key thresholds and choices, and the rules the work must follow, such as what each tool may edit. The developer then reviews every result and runs every git command. Each phase goes in its own branch and pull request.
  • Kiro writes the spec in specs/. It lists what to build (the exact files, functions, messages, and settings), what must not change, the numbers to match, and when to stop and report.
  • Cursor implements the code from the spec: src/, tests/, and running the commands. It keeps a log of what it did, and ends with a report of anything that differs from the spec, any choice the spec did not cover, and the real numbers beside the expected ones.
  • Kiro reviews the result against the spec and the repository. It then adds comments and docstrings to the finished code, and writes the docs. Adding comments does not change behavior, and this is checked by comparing the structure of the code before and after. A number in the docs is recomputed from the data or the code before it is stated.
  • Why this split. A written spec with numbers to match makes the build checkable, and a separate review finds problems the builder would not. Specs are kept in specs/archive/ once they are done.
  • The docs are published with GitHub Pages, built by MkDocs with the Material theme from mkdocs.yml, which is committed. A GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml) builds the site in strict mode and publishes it whenever a change to the docs reaches main. Turned down: keeping the site local only. Publishing needs no extra service, and the README can link to the live pages.
  • A phase gets full pages once it is built, with a brief and an implementation page. Later phases share one high-level page until they begin.
  • The original brief and requirements are kept unchanged in docs/implementation/requirements/, next to the requirements map.

docs.title: Phase 1: Data Pipeline
docs.text:
Docs: nflverse nfldata, requests, pandas, Amazon S3, boto3, IAM.

  • nflverse: the open project that publishes the games file, one row per NFL game since 1999. See the games.csv file.
  • requests: the Python library that downloads the games file.
  • pandas: the Python library that holds the game tables and does the filtering and grouping. It is used in cleaning (Phase 1) and in building the model inputs (Phase 2).
  • NumPy: the Python library for number work that pandas and scikit-learn are built on. See the documentation.
  • Amazon S3: storage for files in the cloud. This project keeps one cleaned table in a private bucket.
  • Bucket and key: a bucket is a named container in S3, and a key is a file's path inside it.
  • boto3: the Python library for calling AWS. It finds credentials itself, from environment variables or ~/.aws, so no key is written in the project.
  • IAM and least privilege: IAM decides who may do what in AWS, and least privilege gives each identity only the access it needs. See the best practices.

docs.title: Phase 2: Features, Training, and Tracking
docs.text: Docs: scikit-learn, MLflow, MLflow tracking, MLflow Models, joblib, skops, matplotlib, SQLite.

docs.title: Features and the Split
docs.text:
• Feature: one input number the model uses. This project has two, both built from earlier games of the same season: win_pct_differential (home win percentage minus away) and point_diff_per_game_differential (home point margin per game minus away).
  • Feature engineering: building features from raw columns. Here, scores and weeks become each team's win percentage and margin so far, then the two differences.
  • Target (label): the answer the model learns to predict, home_win (1 or 0). It is the only column that uses the current game's result.
  • Split by season: training games (2020 to 2024) fit the model, validation games (2025) give the reported score, and test games (2026 weeks 1 to 10) are a final check. Whole seasons go to one group, so the model never trains on games played after the ones it is scored on.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
• Logistic regression: a simple classifier. It multiplies each feature by a learned weight, adds an intercept, and passes the total through an S-shaped function that gives a probability from 0 to 1. See the guide and the LogisticRegression class.
  • Weight and intercept: a weight says how much one feature moves the prediction. The intercept is the starting value, which here captures the average home-field edge.
  • Probability and threshold: the model outputs the chance that the home team wins. Above 0.5 picks the home team, and exactly 0.5 picks the away team.
  • Standardization (scaler): subtracting each feature's average and dividing by its spread, measured on training games only. The two features differ in size by about 30 times, so this lets the model weigh them fairly. See StandardScaler.
  • Pipeline: one object chaining the scaler and the model, so a saved model can never be used without its scaling. See Pipeline.
  • Parameter and hyperparameter: a parameter is learned in training, such as a weight. A hyperparameter is chosen beforehand. Neither is the same as an MLflow parameter, which is a setting written down for a run.
  • Regularization and C: a penalty that holds weights near zero so the model does not memorize the training games. C is the inverse of its strength, so a smaller C is a stronger penalty. The default is 1.0.
  • Solver (lbfgs) and max_iter: the solver finds the best weights by repeatedly adjusting them until the errors stop falling. max_iter caps the adjustments. It finishes in about 6 here, so 1000 is a safety margin.
  • Random seed: a starting number for random choices, so reruns match. The lbfgs solver uses no randomness, so the seed only protects later random steps.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
• Accuracy and baseline: accuracy is the share of games where the pick matches the result. It is shown next to the baseline, the score of always picking the home team. See accuracy_score.
  • Log loss: a score for the probabilities, not just the picks. Each game gets a penalty that is small if the model gave a high chance to what really happened and large if it gave a low one. Lower is better, and saying 50-50 on every game scores 0.6931. It is not logged for training games, because the model is fitted by pushing it down there. See log_loss.
  • Calibration: whether percentages match how often things happen, so 70% should be right about 7 times in 10. Log loss rewards it and accuracy cannot see it. See probability calibration.
  • Confusion matrix: a 2 by 2 table of picks against results. The diagonal holds the correct picks. See confusion_matrix.
  • matplotlib and the Agg backend: matplotlib draws the confusion-matrix image. The Agg backend draws to a file without opening a window.

docs.title: Saving the Model
docs.text:
• joblib: saves a Python object to a file and loads it back. It is the usual way to save a scikit-learn model. See model persistence.
  • pickle: the Python format that joblib builds on. Only load a saved file you trust. See pickle.
  • model.joblib: the working copy of the model, saved with the input names, the model version, the scikit-learn version, and the training seasons. It is the file the API loads.

docs.title: MLflow Tracking
docs.text:
• MLflow: an open-source tool for keeping a record of machine learning work. This project uses its tracking part only: each run writes down its settings, scores, and files. It does not use the model registry or serving tools.
  • Experiment and run: an experiment is a named group of runs (nfl-pregame-winner-v1). A run is one execution of training, with a run ID, a name (LogisticRegression-v1.0), and a status such as FINISHED or FAILED.
  • Parameter (MLflow): a setting written down for a run as text, such as the seed, C, the seasons, the row counts, the scikit-learn version, and the data fingerprint. Each run records 15.
  • Metric: a number written down for a run, such as an accuracy. Each run records 8.
  • Tag: a label on a run. MLflow adds the git commit, branch, repository address, script name, and user itself.
  • Artifact: a file stored with a run. Each run stores three: the saved model file, the confusion-matrix image, and a copy of config.yaml.
  • Backend store: where MLflow keeps experiments, runs, parameters, metrics, and tags. Here it is a database file, mlflow.db. See backend stores.
  • SQLite and the tracking URI: SQLite is a database that lives in one file and needs no server. The tracking URI is the address MLflow uses to find the store, here sqlite:/// plus the full path of mlflow.db. The path starts with /, so the address has four slashes in a row.
  • Artifact store: where MLflow keeps files. Here it is mlartifacts/, with a subfolder per run. The location is set when an experiment is created and cannot be changed afterward. See artifact stores.
  • MLflow model format and flavor: a standard folder layout for a saved model, so MLflow can load it back: a description file (MLmodel), the serialized model, and files listing the needed packages. The flavor names the library that built the model, here scikit-learn. See the scikit-learn flavor.
  • Logged model: in MLflow 3, a model saved in that format is its own entry linked to the run, stored in a models/ folder in the artifact store and not in the run's file list.
  • MLflow UI: a web page for browsing runs, started with mlflow ui --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db. See the tracking UI.
  • Run summary (results/run-summary.json): a small readable record of the latest run, committed to git. It has no run ID, time, or machine path, so it stays identical when the settings and data do not change.

docs.title: Phase 3: Local Prediction API
docs.text:
Built. See the Phase 3 Brief and the Phase 3 Implementation.

Docs: FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, ASGI.

  • FastAPI: the Python library that builds the web service. It routes each request to a function and returns JSON.
  • Pydantic: the library FastAPI uses to check each request's fields, types, and ranges, and to describe the response. A request that fails the checks gets an error before any model code runs.
  • Uvicorn and ASGI: a FastAPI app is only a Python object. It does not listen for requests on its own. Uvicorn is the program that does: it opens a port on the computer, receives each HTTP request, hands it to the app, and sends the app's answer back. They talk through ASGI, the standard interface between Python web servers and Python web apps. Uvicorn is used only on a laptop. On AWS Lambda there is no port to listen on, and Mangum takes its place (Phase 4).
  • Start-up step (lifespan): code that runs once when the app starts. The API loads the saved model there, so each request reuses it.
  • NumPy, not pandas, in the API: the API passes the two inputs to the model as a NumPy array. It does not import pandas, which would push the Lambda zip over its 250 MB limit (278.4 MB with pandas, 231.3 MB without). Training and cleaning still use pandas. See Why Does the API Use NumPy Instead of pandas?.
  • Test client: FastAPI's way to call the app in memory, with no server and no network, so tests run fast.

docs.title: Phase 4: AWS Deployment
docs.text:
Built. See the Phase 4 Brief and the Phase 4 Implementation.

Docs: AWS Lambda, API Gateway, Mangum, Amazon ECR.

  • AWS Lambda: runs code only when a request arrives, with no server to manage.
  • API Gateway: gives the function a public web address, and routes each request to it.
  • Mangum: a small library that translates between the request format AWS Lambda hands a function (a dictionary) and the format FastAPI expects, so the same app runs on a laptop and in Lambda. It does not carry the request to Lambda. API Gateway does that. See What Is Mangum?.
  • Lambda zip and size limit: the function's code and packages are uploaded as a zip. The unzipped size must be 250 MB or less. This project's zip is 231.3 MB without pandas. See the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • Environment variable: a named setting passed to the function when it starts. This function has one, JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING=0, which stops joblib from checking for multiprocessing support that Lambda does not have.
  • CodeSha256: the SHA-256 fingerprint AWS stores for the zip a function was created from. When it equals the hash of the local zip, Lambda is running the file built here.
  • ECR: stores Docker images. It is used only if the Lambda zip turns out to be too large.

  • Vite: the tool that runs the web app on a laptop during development and builds the files that are published.
  • CloudFront: serves the built web app's files over HTTPS from a private S3 bucket.

docs.text:

  • Docker: packages a program with everything it needs, so it runs the same on any machine.
  • Image: the packaged snapshot that Docker builds.
  • Dockerfile and build target: a Dockerfile lists the build steps. It can define several build targets, here train and serve.

docs.title: Phase 7: Documentation and README
docs.text:
Planned. See Remaining Phases.

Docs: MkDocs, Material for MkDocs, Mermaid, GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions.

  • MkDocs: builds the pages in docs/ into a documentation site. A strict build (mkdocs build --strict) fails on a broken link, so it doubles as a link check.
  • Material for MkDocs: the theme that gives the site its layout, navigation, and diagram support.
  • Mermaid: a text format for diagrams, written inside a code block in a page and drawn by the site.
  • GitHub Pages: a GitHub feature that serves a built site from a repository. mkdocs gh-deploy builds the docs and pushes the result to a branch named gh-pages, and Pages serves that branch. See deploying your docs.
  • GitHub Actions: GitHub's built-in way to run a job when something happens in the repository. The workflow .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml runs when docs change on main: it installs MkDocs, runs a strict build, and publishes the site. See the documentation.
  • README: the file at the top of the repository that a visitor reads first. It links to the dataset, the live API, and the live web app.

docs.title: Phase 8: Review
docs.text: Planned. See Remaining Phases. This phase uses no new tools.

docs.title: General Machine Learning Ideas
docs.text:
• Supervised learning: learning from examples that come with known answers. Every game has a known winner, so the model can be checked against answers it has not seen.
  • Binary classification: a task with exactly two possible answers. Here: did the home team win (1) or not (0)? The alternative, regression, predicts a number on a scale. See Why Binary Classification and Not Regression?.
  • Training, validation, and test sets: training data fits the model, validation data gives the score to report, and test data is a final check on games the model never touched.
  • Data leakage: a feature that uses information from after the thing being predicted, which inflates scores. Using only earlier weeks prevents it, and a check stops the run if a week-1 feature is not 0.
  • Overfitting: memorizing the training games instead of learning a pattern that carries over, so the training score is high and the score on unseen games is lower.

docs.title: General Tooling and Reproducibility
docs.text:
Docs: pytest, venv, hashlib, PyYAML.

  • Reproducibility: getting the same result again from the same inputs on any machine. Here it comes from pinned versions, a fixed seed, settings in one file, and a data fingerprint. See Reproducing the Pipeline End to End.
  • Pinned version: an exact version in requirements.txt, such as scikit-learn==1.9.1, so every install is identical. A saved model may fail to load under another scikit-learn version.
  • Virtual environment: a private folder of Python packages for one project, so projects do not interfere.
  • config.yaml: the one file holding every adjustable setting. YAML is a text format of indented name: value lines.
  • Data fingerprint (SHA-256): a short code worked out from every byte of a file. If one byte changes, the code changes, so two runs with the same fingerprint used the same data.
  • pytest and stand-in objects: pytest runs the tests in tests/. The tests use made-up data and stand-ins for the real S3 client and model, so they need no internet and no AWS account.

docs.title: Remaining Phases
docs.text:
Phases 1 to 4 are built. Each has its own pages, the latest being Phase 3 (local API) and Phase 4 (AWS deployment, with an implementation page). Phases 5 to 8 are not started, so this page stays high level. Each phase gets a detailed page when it begins.

The order is: the web app, then Docker, then the documentation and README, then a final review. Docker is after the web app because nothing before it needs an image. AWS Lambda runs the API from a zip file, so there is no container registry unless the zip turns out to be too large (see the Phase 4 Brief). The README and the review come last because they describe and check the finished project.

docs.title: Phase 5: Web App and Hosting
docs.text:
Build the part a person uses.

  • Build a Vite web app. The user picks a home team and an away team, the app calls the API, and it shows the predicted winner and probability.
  • Build the team profiles file (python -m src.profiles), which holds each team's record, win percentage, and point margin per game, so the browser can compute the two inputs.
  • Develop against the local API first. The Vite development server can forward /predict requests to the local API, which avoids needing CORS while working locally. Then point the app at the live API.
  • Host the built files in a private S3 bucket served over HTTPS through CloudFront. Add the CloudFront address to the gateway's CORS settings.

docs.title: Phase 6: Docker
docs.text:
Package the project so it runs from a container.

  • Write a Dockerfile that installs every dependency and has entry points for both training and serving. The image must build and run on a laptop. It uses the same Python version and package pins as everything before it.
  • Check the image gives the same answers. The container must return the same probability as the local API for the worked example.

docs.title: Phase 7: Documentation and README
docs.text:
Write the front door of the repository, and make the docs match the finished project.

  • Write the README with the project overview and goals, the dataset and its link, the model and its result, the cloud services used, setup and usage steps (how to train the model, how to build and test the API locally, and how to deploy to the cloud), and links to the live API and the live web app.
  • Check the docs against the finished code. Every page describes what exists, every number is recomputed from the data or the code, and every link resolves in a strict docs build.
  • Complete the requirements map so every requirement has the file, function, setting, or command that covers it, and the docs page that explains it.
  • Check the comments and docstrings in the code read plainly and match what the code does.
  • Keep the docs site published on GitHub Pages by the deploy-docs.yml workflow, and link it from the README.

docs.title: Phase 8: Review
docs.text:
Check the finished project against the requirements before it is handed in.

  • Walk the acceptance checklist item by item, and write down the evidence for each one.
  • Rebuild from a clean checkout, following only the README. Train, run the tests, and start the API locally, and note anything the README leaves out.
  • Run the pre-commit checks: no secrets or generated files are tracked, local-only files are ignored, relative links resolve, and the docs match the latest code.
  • Review the code and configuration independently, and fix or note each finding.
  • Check the repository contents: code, config.yaml, a dependency file, a Dockerfile, MLflow logging, a clear structure, and at least one merged pull request.
  • Check the live API and the live web app with real requests.

docs.title: Open Decisions
docs.text:
Each shows the proposed answer first.

  • Dockerfile layout. Proposed: one file with train and serve targets. Alternative: two Dockerfiles.
  • Standings in the app. Proposed: one snapshot after 2026 week 10. Alternative: standings for each of weeks 1 to 10 with a week picker.
  • Vite template. Proposed: React with TypeScript. Alternative: plain TypeScript or JavaScript.

The settled hosting and API choices are in Decisions.

docs.title: What Is the Source Data?
docs.text:
• Dataset: nflverse games.csv (link), downloaded from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nflverse/nfldata/master/data/games.csv.
  • Size when downloaded (2026-11-17): 7,548 rows and 46 columns. Each row is one game, from the 1999 season through the 2026 schedule.
  • Why this window: the project uses 2020 through 2026 week 10. That stays within the past decade and uses the most recent data. Week 10 of 2026 is the last week where every game has a score in the file.

docs.title: What Is the Run Environment?
docs.text:
This is the one place the environment is stated. Other pages refer to it.

  • Language: Python 3.13 (the local virtual environment uses 3.13.14). The Lambda function in Phase 4 and the Docker image in Phase 6 must use the same minor version.
  • Python packages: installed from requirements.txt, pinned to exact versions.
  • AWS: an account, AWS CLI version 2, and credentials configured on the machine. Steps 3 and 4 need them.
  • Network: access to GitHub (Step 1) and S3 (Steps 3 and 4).
  • Later phases: Node.js with npm for the Phase 5 web app, and Docker Desktop for Phase 6.
  • Docs: MkDocs with the Material theme, kept out of the project dependency files.

docs.title: What Is the Prediction Task?
docs.text:
The first design choice is the prediction task: classification or regression. It is made in Phase 1 because it decides which rows are usable and which columns are kept.

  • Supervised learning: the model learns from past games where the answer is known, then predicts games where it is not.
  • Classification predicts one of a fixed set of labels. Regression predicts a number on a scale, such as a score margin.
  • This project uses binary classification (two labels): did the home team win? The answer is 1 (home win) or 0 (away win). That answer is the target, in a column called home_win.
  • Why not regression: the web app shows a predicted winner and a win probability. A classifier gives both directly. A margin model would need an extra step to turn a margin into a probability. The full reasoning, with the numbers, is in Decisions.
  • What the task needs from the data:
    • Exactly two outcomes. A tie has neither, so the 6 tied games are removed.
    • Both final scores. home_win is 1 when home_score is greater than away_score. It is built in Phase 2, so the saved table holds only facts from the source file.
    • A finished game for every row. Unplayed games have no answer and are removed.
  • Home-win rate: home teams won 931 of the 1,759 kept games, or 52.93%. Always picking the home team is therefore the baseline the model must beat.

docs.title: Step 1: Fetch the Raw Data and Save It
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Download games.csv and save an unchanged copy as data/raw/games.csv.

Why: nflverse updates this file as games are played and can correct old scores, so a saved copy gives cleaning a fixed input.

If skipped: Two cleaning runs on different days could produce different tables.

src/data/fetch_raw.py downloads with requests into a temporary .partial file. It checks the HTTP status, that the file has at least one row, and that the eight columns cleaning reads are present (game_id, season, game_type, week, home_team, away_team, home_score, away_score). Only then does it rename the file, so a failed download never replaces a good copy.

docs.title: Step 2: Clean the Raw Data and Save the Cleaned Table
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Read the raw file and save data/processed/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv with only the 1,759 games that should be used and the 7 columns later steps need.

Why: The raw file holds playoff games, 21 seasons (1999 to 2019) the project does not use, 122 games not played yet, 6 tied games, and 39 columns the project does not use.

If skipped: Playoff and unplayed games would reach the model, and tied games would have no correct answer.

Run it with python -m src.data.clean. The script reads only the saved raw file and never goes to the internet, so the same raw file always gives the same output.

docs.title: Which Columns Are Kept?
docs.text:
The raw file has 46 columns. Cleaning keeps 7 and drops 39.

  • Kept: game_id, season, week, home_team, away_team, home_score, and away_score.
  • Used to filter, then dropped: game_type. It holds REG (7,239 games), WC (120), DIV (108), CON (54), and SB (27).
  • Dropped, because season and week already say when a game was played: gameday, weekday, and gametime.
  • Dropped, because the kept scores already hold them: result (home minus away score), total (the two scores added), and overtime.
  • Dropped as outside team results: venue columns (location, roof, surface, temp, wind, stadium_id, stadium), betting lines (moneylines, spread, total line, and odds), and people (quarterbacks, coaches, referee).
  • Dropped for now: away_rest, home_rest, and div_game. Rest days are not a model input in this project.
  • Dropped as identifiers from other data sources: old_game_id, gsis, nfl_detail_id, pfr, pff, espn, and ftn.

docs.title: Which Rules Run, and in What Order?
docs.text:
The script prints the row count after each rule, so a reader can see where every removed game went.

  • Start: 7,548 rows, the whole raw file.
  • Rule 1, regular season only (game_type is REG): 7,239 rows left, 309 removed. Playoff games are played under different conditions and give some teams extra games, so they stay out of every team's record.
  • Rule 2, seasons 2020 to 2026: 1,887 rows left, 5,352 removed. These are the 1999 to 2019 seasons. The seasons 2020 to 2026 have 256, 272, 271, 272, 272, 272, and 272 games.
  • Rule 3, cut 2026 after week 10: 1,765 rows left, 122 removed. Weeks 11 to 18 of 2026 have no scores yet.
  • Rule 4, remove tied games: 1,759 rows left, 6 removed. A tie has no winner. The tied games are 2020_03_CIN_PHI, 2021_10_DET_PIT, 2022_01_IND_HOU, 2022_13_WAS_NYG, 2025_04_GB_DAL, and 2026_05_NYG_WAS. Each removed tie leaves a one-game gap in the records of the two teams involved.

Rule 3 runs before the missing-score check on purpose. Unplayed games have blank scores, and checking first would stop the step on those 122 rows. After the week cut, a blank score in a game that should have one is a real problem.

The week cut is window.test_through_week (10) in config/config.yaml, applied to the window.end_season season (2026). If nflverse scores week 11 later, the cleaned table does not change until that number is raised.

docs.title: What Stops the Step?
docs.text:
• No raw file: data/raw/games.csv is missing or empty. The step ends with a short message, not a traceback. The fix is to run Step 1.
  • Blank score or team: after rule 3, any game is missing a score, home team, or away team. The message gives the count and the first five game ids.
  • Wrong number of teams: the table does not hold exactly 32 team codes, which would mean a code changed or the window moved.

docs.title: What Does the Saved Table Look Like?
docs.text:
• game_id: the unique game name (season, week, away team, home team), such as 2020_01_ARI_SF. No id repeats.
  • season and week: whole numbers. Weeks run 1 to 18, and 2026 stops at week 10.
  • home_team and away_team: team codes, such as SF and ARI. 32 different codes appear.
  • home_score and away_score: final points as whole numbers, 0 to 70 for home teams and 0 to 59 for away teams. The raw file stores them as decimals (20.0) because blank scores exist in it. After the checks none are blank.
  • Example first row: 2020_01_ARI_SF,2020,1,SF,ARI,20,24.
  • Order: rows are sorted by season, week, and game_id, so the saved file is identical every run.
  • Values are never edited. Cleaning only removes rows and columns. Neutral-site games, such as international games, stay in with the home label the schedule gives them.
  • Size: 1,759 rows and 63,908 bytes. Rows by season are 255 (2020), 271 (2021), 269 (2022), 272 (2023), 272 (2024), 271 (2025), and 149 (2026, weeks 1 to 10). 2022 has one fewer game than the other full seasons because one game was cancelled.

docs.title: Step 3: Upload the Cleaned Table to S3
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Copy the cleaned table to a private S3 bucket.

Why: The pipeline reads its data from cloud storage, and one shared copy keeps every run on the same data.

If skipped: The pipeline would depend on a file on one laptop.

The bucket is 510-m3-nfl-dataset in us-east-1, and the object key is data/processed/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv. Both come from config.yaml. Only the cleaned table is uploaded.

  • The bucket was created by hand, in the AWS console, with all four public-access blocks on. No script creates it, because only an upload script and a download script are needed. S3 encrypts new objects with AES-256 by default.
  • src/data/upload_to_s3.py uploads the file, then asks S3 for the object's size and compares it with the local file (63,908 bytes). A difference stops the step.
  • A failed AWS call (missing credentials, a wrong bucket name, or no permission) ends the step with boto3's own error message and no traceback.

docs.title: Step 4: Download the Cleaned Table From S3 and Save It
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Download the cleaned table and save it as data/from-s3/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv.

Why: Every later run must start from the S3 copy and not from a file someone saved by hand.

If skipped: A run could use an old or edited local file without anyone knowing.

src/data/download_from_s3.py downloads into a temporary .partial file and renames it when the download finishes, so a failed download never replaces a good local copy. It always downloads again, never reuses an earlier local copy, and prints the row count (1,759). Credentials come from the standard AWS credential chain and are never stored in the repository. Step 2 already checked the table, so this step does not check it again. Steps 1 to 3 run once, when the data changes. Anyone who only trains starts at Step 4.

docs.title: What Does Phase 1 Create?
docs.text:
• Code: src/config.py reads config/config.yaml, so no script hard-codes a season, path, or bucket. The four steps live in src/data/, one file per step, in run order: fetch_raw.py, clean.py, upload_to_s3.py, and download_from_s3.py. Later phases add their own folders next to it.
  • Run commands: python -m src.data.fetch_raw, python -m src.data.clean, python -m src.data.upload_to_s3, and python -m src.data.download_from_s3.
  • Settings: config/config.yaml has a data block (source address, the three file paths, bucket, S3 key, region) and a window block (start_season 2020, end_season 2026, test_through_week 10).
  • Other files: requirements.txt (exact versions), pytest.ini, and tests in tests/test_clean.py and tests/test_upload.py.
  • Local data files: data/raw/games.csv (7,548 rows, 46 columns), data/processed/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv (1,759 rows, 7 columns), and data/from-s3/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv (identical to the cleaned table).
  • In AWS: the bucket 510-m3-nfl-dataset in us-east-1. It is private, has all four public-access blocks on, uses AES-256 encryption, and holds one object (63,908 bytes).

docs.title: Which Choices Were Made?
docs.text:
• Only the cleaned table goes to S3. The raw file stays on the developer machine, because only the cleaned data needs to be in the cloud.
  • Training always starts from the S3 copy. The download step fetches again and never reuses an earlier local copy.
  • AWS only. Turned down: Google Cloud and Azure.
  • Two small S3 scripts: upload (checks the object size) and download. Each ends with a short message on an AWS error. Turned down: a shared file that sorted AWS errors into named causes. boto3's own messages already say the same thing.
  • The bucket is created by hand, not by code. Turned down: a setup script. A script that creates AWS resources adds risk for no benefit.
  • Binary classification, not regression. Turned down: predicting the score margin. See Why Binary Classification and Not Regression?.
  • Ties are removed (6 games). Turned down: labeling a tie as an away win, and counting a tie as half a win.
  • Playoffs and unplayed games are removed, and the week cap is a setting, not a code edit.
  • Dependencies are pinned to exact versions.
  • No notebooks. They repeated what the scripts and these pages say.

docs.title: Phase 2 Brief: Features, Training, and Tracking
docs.text:
Status: Built and tested. All 7 steps are done, and pytest passes 30 tests. Needs first: Phase 1, which is built. Its output is the downloaded table data/from-s3/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv.

Phase 2 turns the cleaned games into two inputs per game, trains the model, and keeps a record of every run. It fits a logistic regression on the 2020 to 2024 games, scores it on the 2025 season and on the 2026 test games, and saves the settings, scores, and files of each run in MLflow.

docs.title: Steps in Order
docs.text:
• Step 1. Feature engineering: build the two inputs in src/model/features.py: home minus away win percentage, and home minus away point margin per game, both from earlier weeks of the same season.
  • Step 2. Split the games by season. Training 2020 to 2024, validation 2025, test 2026 weeks 1 to 10.
  • Step 3. Add the model and tracking settings to config/config.yaml.
  • Step 4. Fit the scaler and the model on the training seasons only. Save both as one scikit-learn pipeline.
  • Step 5. Score the model. Accuracy on the training, validation, and test games, next to the baseline. Also log loss and one plot.
  • Step 6. Record the run in MLflow: settings, scores, and files, plus an MLflow-format copy of the model.
  • Step 7. Save the final pipeline as models/model.joblib, write the readable run summary results/run-summary.json, and add models/, mlflow.db, and mlartifacts/ to .gitignore.

docs.title: Details in Brief
docs.text:
• Inputs: a team with no games yet counts as win percentage 0.5 and margin 0.0, so week 1 gives 0 for both inputs. Reasons for raw values over ranks are in Decisions.
  • Split: training is 1,339 games, validation is 271, and test is 149. The test games never fit anything. With only 149 of them, their accuracy can move by about 4 points by chance.
  • Baseline: always picking the home team scores 53.32% on training, 53.87% on 2025, and 47.65% on the test games. The model must beat this.
  • One saved object: the scaler and the model travel together in one pipeline, so the API cannot apply the model without the scaler. The scaler learns its averages from training rows only.
  • Tracking: a local database file mlflow.db, with run files in mlartifacts/. Each run records 15 parameters (including the scikit-learn version and a fingerprint of the data file), 8 scores, 3 files, and an MLflow-format copy of the model.
  • Readable record: each run also writes results/run-summary.json, which is committed to git and stays identical when the settings and data do not change.
  • Logistic regression only. There is no model comparison. Random forest and XGBoost are left out, which keeps the model simple to explain and the serving image small.

docs.title: What Was Created
docs.text:
• Settings: new split, model, and tracking blocks in config/config.yaml, including tracking.summary_path.
  • Code: src/model/features.py, src/model/train.py, and src/model/evaluate.py, next to the Phase 1 folder src/data/, with tests in tests/. Packages matplotlib and joblib are pinned in requirements.txt.
  • Committed: results/run-summary.json.
  • Local only, not committed: mlflow.db, the mlartifacts/ folder, and models/model.joblib.

docs.title: Step 1: Feature Engineering
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Turn each game into two numbers the model can learn from, plus the answer it should predict. Building input numbers (features) from raw columns is called feature engineering.

Why: The model cannot read team names. It needs numbers that say how the home team compares with the away team going into the game.

If skipped: There would be nothing to train on.

docs.title: Which Functions Do the Work?
docs.text:
All of these are in src/model/features.py. Everything is built in memory on each run, and no new data file is saved.

  • load_games(config) reads the downloaded table, and stops with a message to run the download step first if the file is missing.
  • standings_before_week(games, season, week, teams) returns one row per team, counting only earlier weeks of that season.
  • build_model_table(games) returns one row per game with the two inputs and the answer.
  • check_model_table(table) stops the run if an input is blank or any week-1 input is not exactly 0.
  • split_games(table, config) is Step 2.

docs.title: What Is Counted Before Each Game?
docs.text:
• Earlier weeks of the same season only. For a game in week 7 of 2025, each team's numbers come from its games in weeks 1 to 6 of 2025. Games in week 7 itself are never counted, so a game cannot be described by its own result or by another result from the same week.
  • Numbers start over every season. A team's 2024 results are not used in 2025.
  • Win percentage: wins divided by games played so far.
  • Point margin per game: points scored minus points allowed so far, divided by games played so far.
  • A team with no games yet counts as win percentage 0.5 and point margin 0.0. This happens for every team in week 1.
  • Per game, not season totals. Teams have played different numbers of games by mid-season because of bye weeks. Before week 8 of 2025, 23 teams had played 7 games, 8 teams had played 6, and 1 team had played 5. A season total would favor the teams that had played more games.
  • Tied games are not in the table. Phase 1 removed them, so two teams in a removed game show one fewer game.

docs.title: What Do the Standings Look Like?
docs.text:
Standings before week 7 of 2025 for a few teams. Twenty-five teams had played 6 games, six had played 5, and Green Bay had played 4.

docs.title: How Are the Standings Built?
docs.text:
def standings_before_week(games, season, week, teams):
    """One row per team from games played earlier in this season."""
    # Same-week games are left out, so a result cannot describe itself or the other game that week.
    earlier = games.loc[(games["season"] == season) & (games["week"] < week)]
    rows = []
    for team in teams:
        home = earlier.loc[earlier["home_team"] == team]
        away = earlier.loc[earlier["away_team"] == team]
        played = len(home) + len(away)
        # No games yet would make a percentage undefined. 0.5 and 0 leave week 1 as a tie.
        if played == 0:
            wins = 0
            win_pct = 0.5
            margin = 0.0
        else:
            wins = int((home["home_score"] > home["away_score"]).sum()) + int(
                (away["away_score"] > away["home_score"]).sum()
            )
            scored = float(home["home_score"].sum() + away["away_score"].sum())
            allowed = float(home["away_score"].sum() + away["home_score"].sum())
            # Divide by games played, not a season total, because bye weeks leave teams on different game counts.
            win_pct = wins / played
            margin = (scored - allowed) / played
        rows.append({"team": team, "games": played, "wins": wins,
                     "win_pct": float(win_pct), "point_diff_per_game": float(margin)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

A game counts for both teams. The home team's points scored are home_score, and the away team's are away_score.

docs.title: What Does Each Game Become?
docs.text:
Column Type What it means Example (2025_07_NE_TEN) game_id text Season, week, away team, home team 2025_07_NE_TEN season whole number Season year 2025 week whole number Week of the regular season 7 home_team text Home team code TEN away_team text Away team code NE win_pct_differential decimal Home win percentage minus away win percentage -0.5 point_diff_per_game_differential decimal Home margin per game minus away margin per game -18.0 home_win whole number 1 if home_score is greater than away_score, otherwise 0 0
  • A positive differential means the home team looks stronger. A negative one means the away team does.
  • home_win is the answer the model learns to predict. It is the only column that uses the current game's result, and it is never an input.
  • The model uses only the two differential columns. The other columns identify the game.
  • Rows are sorted by season, week, and game_id.
def build_model_table(games):
    """One row per game, with the two pre-game differentials and the home-win answer."""
    teams = sorted(set(games["home_team"]) | set(games["away_team"]))
    rows = []
    for (season, week), week_games in games.groupby(["season", "week"], sort=False):
        # Once per week, then reused for every game in that week.
        standings = standings_before_week(games, int(season), int(week), teams).set_index("team")
        for game in week_games.itertuples(index=False):
            home = standings.loc[game.home_team]
            away = standings.loc[game.away_team]
            rows.append({
                "game_id": game.game_id,
                "season": int(game.season),
                "week": int(game.week),
                "home_team": game.home_team,
                "away_team": game.away_team,
                "win_pct_differential": float(home["win_pct"] - away["win_pct"]),
                "point_diff_per_game_differential": float(
                    home["point_diff_per_game"] - away["point_diff_per_game"]
                ),
                "home_win": int(game.home_score > game.away_score),
            })
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=MODEL_COLUMNS)
    return table.sort_values(["season", "week", "game_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)

docs.title: How Do the Inputs Behave?
docs.text:
• Ranges across all 1,759 games: win_pct_differential runs from -1.0 to 1.0, and point_diff_per_game_differential runs from -49.0 to 39.0. Neither has a blank value.
  • All games: win_pct_differential has an average of -0.0045 and a spread (standard deviation) of 0.3598. point_diff_per_game_differential has an average of -0.2317 and a spread of 10.1942.
  • Training games only: the averages are -0.0004 and -0.1762, and the spreads are 0.3476 and 10.1117. Part 2 uses these when it standardizes the inputs.
  • The two inputs overlap. Their correlation in the training games is 0.78, because teams that win more tend to have better margins. Logistic regression handles this.
  • The scales differ by about 30 times, which is why Part 2 standardizes the inputs before the model sees them.
  • When both inputs agree, the home team usually follows them. In 574 games both inputs are positive, and the home team won 69.51% of them. In 604 games both are negative, and the home team won 36.92%. In 196 games the two inputs point opposite ways, and 115 games have both inputs at 0 (111 in week 1 and 4 later).

docs.title: What Happens in Week 1?
docs.text:
• Before week 1 no team has played, so every team counts as 0.5 and 0.0, and both inputs are exactly 0 for all 111 week-1 games (79 training, 16 validation, 16 test).
  • The model cannot tell those games apart, so it will pick the home team in all of them.
  • Week 1 games are kept in the data like every other week.

docs.title: How Is the Week-1 Rule Enforced?
docs.text:
def check_model_table(table):
    """Stop if a model input is blank or a week-1 differential is not zero."""
    if table[INPUT_COLUMNS].isna().any().any():

    week_one = table.loc[table["week"] == 1, INPUT_COLUMNS]
    if (week_one != 0).any().any():
        raise ValueError("a week-1 differential is not 0")

docs.title: Step 2: Split the Games by Season
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Split the games into training, validation, and test groups by season.

Why: The model must predict games that have not happened yet. It learns from earlier seasons, is scored on a later finished season, and is also shown the season in progress.

If skipped: A random split would train on later games and score on earlier ones, and the scores could not be trusted.

docs.title: Which Games Go in Each Group?
docs.text:
Group Seasons Games Weeks Home wins Home win share Training 2020 to 2024 1,339 1 to 18 714 53.32% Validation 2025 271 1 to 18 146 53.87% Test 2026 149 1 to 10 71 47.65%
  • Training is the only group the model is fit on.
  • Validation is the last finished season. It is never used to fit the model, and it gives the score to report.
  • Test is the season in progress, cut to the weeks that have scores. It is never used to fit the model. With only 149 games, its accuracy can move by about 4 points either way by chance.
  • Always picking the home team is the baseline in the last column. The model has to beat it to add anything.
  • Week 1 games: 79 are in training, 16 in validation, and 16 in test.
  • Games by season: 255 (2020), 271 (2021), 269 (2022), 272 (2023), 272 (2024), 271 (2025), and 149 (2026). A full season has 272 games. 2020 had 256 (its last week was week 17), and 2022 had 271 because one game was cancelled. Each season then loses its tied games: one each in 2020, 2021, and 2025, two in 2022, and one in 2026.
  • Why by season, not at random: each season stands on its own, because the numbers start over each year. Splitting whole seasons also keeps every game in a group from using results that came after the games in the next group.

docs.title: How Are the Seasons Chosen?
docs.text:
The test season and the week cap come from the existing window block, and only two seasons are new in split, so no season is written in two places.

def split_seasons(config):
    """First training season, last training season, validation season, and test season."""
    start_season, test_season, _test_week = season_window(config)
    train_end_season = int(config["split"]["train_end_season"])
    validation_season = int(config["split"]["validation_season"])
    if start_season > train_end_season:
        raise ValueError(
            f"first training season {start_season} is after last training season {train_end_season}"
        )
    if train_end_season >= validation_season:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validation season {validation_season} is not after last training season {train_end_season}"
        )
    if validation_season >= test_season:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validation season {validation_season} is not before test season {test_season}"
        )
    return start_season, train_end_season, validation_season, test_season

With the real settings this returns (2020, 2024, 2025, 2026). A season order that would score the model on a season it already trained on is rejected with a message.

docs.title: How Is the Table Split?
docs.text:
def split_games(table, config):
    """Training, validation, and test tables, one season range each."""
    start_season, train_end_season, validation_season, test_season = split_seasons(config)
    groups = {
        "training": table.loc[table["season"].between(start_season, train_end_season)].copy(),
        "validation": table.loc[table["season"] == validation_season].copy(),
        "test": table.loc[table["season"] == test_season].copy(),
    }
    for name, group in groups.items():
        if group.empty:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} has no rows")
    game_ids = [set(group["game_id"]) for group in groups.values()]
    combined = set.union(*game_ids)
    # A season that falls in a gap, or a game id that lands in two groups, would make the sizes disagree.
    if sum(len(ids) for ids in game_ids) != len(combined) or len(combined) != len(table):
        raise ValueError("every game must be in exactly one split group")
    return groups
  • An empty group stops the run with a message that names the group, such as validation has no rows.
  • Every game must land in exactly one group, so the three sizes always add up to 1,759.

docs.title: Step 3: Add the Model and Tracking Settings
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Put every new tunable value for Phase 2 into config/config.yaml.

Why: Changing a run should mean editing the settings file, not the code.

If skipped: Seasons, model values, and file names would be written inside the code.

Three new blocks sit below the existing data and window blocks. Those two blocks did not change.

# How the games are split by season. Training starts at window.start_season (2020) and stops
# at train_end_season. The validation season is the finished season after it, and its score is
# the one to report. The test season is window.end_season, so that year is not written here
# a second time. The model is fit on the training seasons only.
split:
  train_end_season: 2024
  validation_season: 2025

# The model and how it is saved.
model:
  # A label for this trained model. It is saved inside the model file and in the MLflow run.
  version: v1.0
  # A starting number for any random choice, so a rerun gives the same result. The solver
  # below does not use randomness, so two fits match either way. The seed is kept so a random
  # step added later stays repeatable.
  random_seed: 42
  # Where the trained model is saved.
  output_path: models/model.joblib
  # Logistic regression: the model gives each input a weight, adds them up, and turns the
  # total into a chance (0 to 1) that the home team wins.
  logistic_regression:
    # How strongly the weights are held close to zero, to stop the model from memorizing the
    # training games. A smaller number holds them tighter. 1.0 is the usual starting point.
    C: 1.0
    # The method that finds the best weights. "lbfgs" repeatedly nudges the weights to lower
    # the model's errors until they stop improving. It suits a small table like this one.
    solver: lbfgs
    # The most nudges the solver may make before it gives up. The solver finishes in about 6
    # here, so 1000 leaves a wide safety margin.
    max_iter: 1000

# MLflow, the tool that records every training run so runs can be compared later.
tracking:
  # The name that groups every run of this project.
  experiment_name: nfl-pregame-winner-v1
  # The database file where MLflow keeps each run's settings and scores.
  database_path: mlflow.db
  # The folder where MLflow keeps each run's files (the model, the plot, a copy of this file).
  artifact_folder: mlartifacts
  # A small readable summary of the latest run (settings, data fingerprint, scores, and the
  # learned weights). It is committed to git. MLflow keeps the full history of runs.
  summary_path: results/run-summary.json

docs.title: What Does Each Setting Do?
docs.text:
• split.train_end_season: the last training season (2024). Training starts at window.start_season (2020).
  • split.validation_season: the validation season (2025). The test season is window.end_season (2026), and window.test_through_week (10) is already applied by cleaning.
  • model.version: a label for the trained model (v1.0). It is saved with the model and shown by the API later.
  • model.random_seed: the starting number for any random choice (42). The lbfgs solver does not use randomness, so two fits give the same result either way. The seed is kept so any later random step stays repeatable.
  • model.output_path: where the trained model is saved (models/model.joblib).
  • model.logistic_regression.C: regularization strength (1.0). A smaller value pulls the weights toward zero more strongly. This is scikit-learn's default.
  • model.logistic_regression.solver: the method that finds the weights (lbfgs).
  • model.logistic_regression.max_iter: the most steps the solver may take (1000), set high enough that it always finishes.
  • tracking.experiment_name: the MLflow group that holds every run (nfl-pregame-winner-v1).
  • tracking.database_path: the database file that holds the run record (mlflow.db).
  • tracking.artifact_folder: the folder that holds each run's files (mlartifacts).
  • tracking.summary_path: where each run writes its readable summary (results/run-summary.json). See What Is the Run Summary File?.

docs.title: Where Does MLflow Keep Its Records?
docs.text:
• A database file. MLflow stores each run's settings and scores in a local database file, mlflow.db. It is a single file, it needs no server, and it is not committed to git.
  • A folder of files. Each run's files (the model, the plot, and a copy of the settings) go in mlartifacts/, in a subfolder for each run.
  • The tracking address. The only place the database type shows up is the address MLflow requires, which starts with sqlite:/// followed by the full path of mlflow.db.
