docs.title: Step 4: Fit the Scaler and the Model
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Learn the model from the training games, and keep the scaler and the model together as one object.

Why: The two inputs are on very different scales (about 0.35 versus about 10). Standardizing them first lets the model weigh them fairly, and keeping both in one object means the API cannot apply the model without the scaler.

If skipped: There would be no model to score or serve.

docs.title: How Is the Pipeline Built?
docs.text:
def build_pipeline(config: dict):
    """A scaler and a logistic regression, with every setting taken from the config file."""
    logistic = config["model"]["logistic_regression"]
    return make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        LogisticRegression(
            C=logistic["C"],
            solver=logistic["solver"],
            max_iter=logistic["max_iter"],
            random_state=config["model"]["random_seed"],
        ),
    )


def fit_pipeline(config: dict, training):
    """Fit the scaler and the model on the training games only."""
    pipeline = build_pipeline(config)
    # Validation and test games stay out of this call, so their results cannot move the weights.
    pipeline.fit(training[INPUT_COLUMNS], training["home_win"])
    return pipeline
  • Training rows only. The scaler's averages and spreads, and the model's weights, come from the 1,339 training games. Validation and test games never touch the fit.
  • Named columns. The inputs are passed as a table with the two column names, not as a bare array, so the order of the inputs is fixed and the API can rely on it.
  • Every value comes from config.yaml. Nothing about the model is written in the code.

docs.title: What Does the Fit Learn?
docs.text:
• The scaler learns one average and one spread for each input, from the training games:
    • win_pct_differential: average -0.0004, spread 0.3476
    • point_diff_per_game_differential: average -0.1762, spread 10.1117
  • The model learns one weight for each standardized input, plus an intercept:
    • weight for win_pct_differential: 0.2138
    • weight for point_diff_per_game_differential: 0.3081
    • intercept: 0.1403
    • The solver finished in 6 steps (the limit is 1000).
  • Reading the weights: both are positive, so a stronger home team on either input raises the home win probability. The margin input has the larger weight.
  • Reading the intercept: it is positive, which is the home-field edge. With both inputs at 0, the home win probability is 0.5364. Home teams won 53.32% of the training games.
  • Repeatable: a second fit with the same settings gives identical probabilities.

docs.title: What Is a Worked Example?
docs.text:
Game 2025_07_NE_TEN has inputs -0.5 and -18.0. The scaler turns them into standardized values, and the model adds them up:

  • Standardized win percentage input: (-0.5 - (-0.0004)) / 0.3476 = about -1.44.
  • Standardized margin input: (-18.0 - (-0.1762)) / 10.1117 = about -1.76.
  • Weighted sum: 0.1403 + 0.2138 x (-1.44) + 0.3081 x (-1.76) = about -0.71.
  • The logistic function turns -0.71 into a probability of about 0.33.

The model's own output for this game is 0.3296, a 33% chance that Tennessee wins. That is below 0.5, so the prediction is an away win. New England won, so it is correct.

docs.title: Step 5: Score the Model
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Measure how often the model picks the winner, and compare it with the always-pick-home baseline.

Why: A score on its own means little. Beating a simple rule shows the inputs add something.

If skipped: There would be no result to report.

docs.title: How Is a Game Scored?
docs.text:
• The model gives a home win probability for each game. A probability above 0.5 is a pick for the home team, and anything else is a pick for the away team.
  • Two scores are used, and each answers a different question:
    • Accuracy: how often is the pick right?
    • Log loss: are the percentages the model gives believable?
  • Baseline is the score of always picking the home team, which is the share of games the home team won.
  • Safeguard: log loss is always given the labels [0, 1], so a group with only one outcome does not raise an error.
def score_group(pipeline, group) -> dict:
    """Accuracy, the always-home baseline, and log loss for one group."""
    # Keep the column names so the pipeline applies the inputs in the saved order.
    probability = pipeline.predict_proba(group[INPUT_COLUMNS])[:, 1]
    # Exactly 0.5 is an away pick. Only a higher probability picks the home team.
    picked_home = (probability > 0.5).astype(int)
    home_win = group["home_win"].to_numpy()
    games = int(len(group))
    correct = int((picked_home == home_win).sum())
    return {
        "games": games,
        "correct": correct,
        "accuracy": correct / games,
        "baseline": float((home_win == 1).mean()),
        "log_loss": float(log_loss(home_win, probability, labels=[0, 1])),
    }

docs.title: What Is Accuracy?
docs.text:
Accuracy is the share of games where the model's pick matches the real result. It is the headline number the project reports, and it is shown next to the baseline so a reader can see whether the model adds anything.

Group Games Correct Accuracy Always pick home Training 1,339 820 61.24% 53.32% Validation 271 171 63.10% 53.87% Test 149 88 59.06% 47.65%
  • The model beats the baseline in every group: by 7.9 points on training, 9.2 on validation, and 11.4 on test.
  • The validation score is the one to report. It is a finished season the model never saw.
  • The test score is noisy. With 149 games, accuracy can move by about 4 points either way by chance. The test baseline is low (47.65%) because home teams won fewer than half of those games.
  • The score is reported whatever it is, even if it is poor.
  • What accuracy cannot see: a pick of "home team, 51% chance" and a pick of "home team, 90% chance" count the same. Log loss looks at what accuracy ignores.

docs.title: What Is Log Loss?
docs.text:
Short answer: a high log loss is bad, and a low one is good. It works like a golf score. It is a penalty, so lower is better.

In plain words: for every game, the model gives a percentage chance that the home team wins. After the game, look at how much chance the model had given to what really happened. If it gave the real result a high chance, the penalty is small. If it gave the real result a low chance, the penalty is large. Log loss is the average penalty over all the games.

  • A high log loss means the model was often surprised. It kept giving low chances to things that then happened, usually by being sure of itself and wrong.
  • A low log loss means the model was rarely surprised, so its percentages matched what happened.

How to read the number

  • 0 is the best possible, and it would mean the model gave 100% to every real result. It never happens in practice.
  • 0.6931 is what a model that knows nothing scores. It is the penalty for saying "50-50" about every game.
  • Above 0.6931 is worse than knowing nothing, because the model is confidently wrong too often.
  • Between 0 and 0.6931 means the model has learned something. Football games are hard to predict, so a model that is honest about its uncertainty stays fairly close to 0.69.
  • This model: 0.6451 on validation and 0.6815 on the test set. Both are below 0.6931, so it has learned something. The test number is only a little below, which fits a small set of 149 games.

How the penalty works. It depends on how much chance the model gave to what actually happened. Say the home team won:

  • The model said 90%: penalty 0.11 (small).
  • The model said 70%: penalty 0.36.
  • The model said 50%: penalty 0.69.
  • The model said 30%: penalty 1.20.
  • The model said 10%: penalty 2.30 (large).

Why accuracy is not enough. Two models can pick the same winners and still score very differently. Say both pick the home team in three games, and the home team wins two and loses one. Both have the same accuracy, 2 of 3.

  • Model A says 60% each time. Its penalties are 0.51, 0.51, and 0.92, so its log loss is 0.646.
  • Model B says 95% each time. Its penalties are 0.05, 0.05, and 3.00, so its log loss is 1.033.

Model B is worse because the one game it lost cost a huge penalty. Log loss rewards a model for saying "50-50" when it does not know, and for saving high percentages for games where it has a reason.

Why it matters here. The web app shows a win probability, not only a pick. Log loss is the check that those percentages mean something, which accuracy cannot tell you.

Does the model's confidence mean anything? Yes.

  • In 2025, the model gave one team at least a 65% chance in 66 games, and it picked the winner in 75.76% of them. In the other 205 games, where it was less sure, it was right 59.02% of the time.
  • In the test set, it was at least 65% sure in 43 games and right in 62.79%, against 57.55% in the other 106.

A game that hurt. In 2025, 2025_03_GB_CLE, the model gave Cleveland (home) only a 23.1% chance, and Cleveland won. That one game had a penalty of 1.46, the largest in the validation season. In the test set, 2026_02_JAX_DEN was the largest at 1.99, with Denver given a 13.7% chance.

Why it is not logged for the training games. Logistic regression is fitted by pushing this very number down on the training games. A low training log loss is expected and says little. Only games the model never saw are a fair check.

Group Model Always 50% Always the home win rate Validation 0.6451 0.6931 0.6902 Test 0.6815 0.6931 0.6985

"Always the home win rate" means saying 53.32% (the training share) for every game. The model is lower, which is better, than both on both groups.

docs.title: How Do the Two Scores Fit Together?
docs.text:
• Accuracy is the headline: how often the model picks the winner, next to the always-pick-home baseline.
  • Log loss supports it: it checks that the probabilities the web app will show are believable.
  • Both are reported for validation and test, and only accuracy for training.

docs.title: What Does the Confusion Matrix Show?
docs.text:
Validation 2025, with the actual result down the side and the model's pick across the top:

Actual result Picked away win Picked home win Away team won (125 games) 62 63 Home team won (146 games) 37 109

The model picks the home team in 172 of 271 games (63.5%), more often than home teams actually win (53.87%). The 171 correct picks are the 62 and the 109.

docs.title: Which Plot Is Drawn?
docs.text:
One image is drawn for the validation season with matplotlib's non-window drawing mode (Agg), so no window opens. It is saved to a temporary folder, stored in the MLflow run, and then removed, so no image is left in the project.

  • confusion_matrix_validation.png: the table above as a heat map, with the count written in each cell.
  • Wording: the title is bold ("Validation 2025: Predicted vs Actual", with the year read from the games in the group), a one-line takeaway under it says how many games were picked correctly (171 of 271), and both axis labels are bold.
def plot_confusion_matrix(pipeline, group, path) -> Path:
    """Save the group's confusion matrix and return the image path."""
    probability = pipeline.predict_proba(group[INPUT_COLUMNS])[:, 1]
    # The same 0.5 rule as the score, so the picture counts the same picks.
    picked_home = (probability > 0.5).astype(int)
    matrix = confusion_matrix(group["home_win"], picked_home, labels=[0, 1])
    figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.5))
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(matrix, display_labels=["Away win", "Home win"]).plot(
        ax=axes,
        colorbar=False,
        cmap="Blues",
        values_format="d",
    )
    # The year comes from the games in this group, so a different validation season renames the figure.
    season = int(group["season"].iloc[0])
    correct = int((picked_home == group["home_win"].to_numpy()).sum())
    figure.suptitle(f"Validation {season}: Predicted vs Actual", fontweight="bold")
    axes.set_title(f"{correct} of {len(group)} games were picked correctly")
    axes.set_xlabel(axes.get_xlabel(), fontweight="bold")
    axes.set_ylabel(axes.get_ylabel(), fontweight="bold")
    destination = Path(path)
    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    figure.savefig(destination, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(figure)
    return destination

docs.title: Step 6: Record the Run in MLflow
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Save the settings, scores, and files of every training run, so runs can be compared and traced.

Why: Each run's settings, scores, and files (the saved model and the plot) are recorded, so any run can be compared and traced later.

If skipped: There would be no record of which settings produced which scores.

docs.title: How Is MLflow Set Up?
docs.text:
This is the first half of log_run in src/model/train.py. It also takes the fitted pipeline, which it stores in MLflow's own model format (see below).

def log_run(config: dict, scores: dict, files: dict, pipeline) -> str:
    """Record one run's settings, scores, and files, and return the run name."""
    database = resolve_path(config["tracking"]["database_path"])
    artifacts = resolve_path(config["tracking"]["artifact_folder"])
    # MLflow keeps its records in a local database file. The address is "sqlite://" plus the
    # full path (which starts with "/"), so it has four slashes in a row.
    mlflow.set_tracking_uri(f"sqlite:///{database}")
    experiment_name = config["tracking"]["experiment_name"]
    # An experiment is the named group that holds every run. Its file folder can only be set
    # when it is created, so create it once and let later runs join it.
    if mlflow.get_experiment_by_name(experiment_name) is None:
        artifacts.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        mlflow.create_experiment(experiment_name, artifact_location=artifacts.as_uri())
    mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_name)
  • The run record goes in the database file mlflow.db, and each run's files go under mlartifacts/<run id>/artifacts/.
  • Run again, and a new run is added to the same experiment. Two runs with the same settings and data give the same scores, and only the run ids differ.

docs.title: What Is Logged for Each Run?
docs.text:
This is the second half of log_run.

    start_season, train_end_season, validation_season, test_season = split_seasons(config)
    model = config["model"]
    logistic = model["logistic_regression"]
    run_name = f"LogisticRegression-{model['version']}"
    # A run that fails partway is closed by `with` and marked as failed, so it is never left open.
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name=run_name):
        # MLflow keeps every parameter as text. Scores below are numbers, so they can be charted.
        mlflow.log_params(
            {
                "model_version": model["version"],
                "random_seed": model["random_seed"],
                "C": logistic["C"],
                "solver": logistic["solver"],
                "max_iter": logistic["max_iter"],
                "feature_names": ",".join(INPUT_COLUMNS),
                "train_start_season": start_season,
                "train_end_season": train_end_season,
                "validation_season": validation_season,
                "test_season": test_season,
                "n_train": scores["training"]["games"],
                "n_validation": scores["validation"]["games"],
                "n_test": scores["test"]["games"],
                "scikit_learn_version": sklearn.__version__,
                "data_sha256": file_fingerprint(data_file(config, "from_s3_path")),
            }
        )
        mlflow.log_metrics({...})  # the 8 scores listed below
        mlflow.log_artifact(str(files["model"]), artifact_path="model")
        mlflow.log_artifact(str(files["plot"]), artifact_path="plots")
        mlflow.log_artifact(str(files["config"]), artifact_path="config")
        mlflow.sklearn.log_model(pipeline, name=MLFLOW_MODEL_NAME)
    return run_name
  • Run name: LogisticRegression-v1.0, the model type and the version label.
  • Settings (parameters), 15 in all: model_version, random_seed, C, solver, max_iter, feature_names, train_start_season, train_end_season, validation_season, test_season, n_train (1339), n_validation (271), n_test (149), scikit_learn_version (1.9.1), and data_sha256.
  • data_sha256: a fingerprint of the downloaded table, worked out from every byte of the file by file_fingerprint. If one byte of the data changes, the code changes, so two runs with the same fingerprint used the same data. For the current table it is 7219e8a8672b900af9facbb54d8a28f9f2a34df9ede3b8385a735768082517fb.
  • Scores (metrics), 8 in all, stored as fractions: train_accuracy, validation_accuracy, test_accuracy, validation_log_loss, test_log_loss, baseline_train, baseline_validation, and baseline_test. Training log loss is left out, because the model is fit by pushing that number down.
  • Files (artifacts), 3 in all: model/model.joblib, plots/confusion_matrix_validation.png, and config/config.yaml, a copy of the settings used.
  • Logged model, 1: an MLflow-format copy of the pipeline, named pipeline-mlflow-format. See the next section.
  • Automatic tags: MLflow also records the git commit, branch, and repository address on every run.
  • Read back from the real run: the one recorded run shows 15 parameters, 8 metrics, the 3 files, and 1 logged model.

docs.title: Why Is the Model Stored Twice?
docs.text:
Each run keeps the trained pipeline in two forms, for two different readers.

  • model/model.joblib is the working copy. It is a plain file in the run's file list. It is what the API will load, and it carries the input names, the model version, the scikit-learn version, and the training seasons.
  • The MLflow-format copy lets MLflow's own screen and loader open the model with one call (mlflow.sklearn.load_model). No project code loads it. Only its test does.
  • Where the MLflow copy lives: MLflow 3 records it as a separate logged model linked to the run, not in the run's file list. Its files are in mlartifacts/models/m-<id>/artifacts/: MLmodel (the description), model.skops (the model, about 25 KB), conda.yaml, python_env.yaml, and requirements.txt (the packages it needs).
  • Same model: both copies come from the same fitted pipeline in the same call, so they cannot disagree. The MLflow copy reloads with identical probabilities.

docs.title: How Is MLflow Kept Tidy?
docs.text:
• Quiet start-up. MLflow prints a hint about its tracing helper when it is imported. This project does not use tracing, so train.py sets MLFLOW_DISABLE_AGENT_HINT before the import and the command prints nothing extra.
  • No leftovers from tests. The tests point MLflow at a temporary database and artifact folder, and each test puts the earlier tracking address back afterward, so no test affects the next one or writes into the project.
  • One hidden warning. MLflow's own database code uses a SQLAlchemy option that SQLAlchemy plans to remove. pytest.ini hides that single warning, because it comes from inside MLflow and not from this project.
  • Where records are kept. See Where Does MLflow Keep Its Records?.

To browse the recorded runs, start the MLflow viewer and open the address it prints:

mlflow ui --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db

docs.title: Step 7: Save the Final Pipeline
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Write the trained pipeline to models/model.joblib, with the facts the API needs to load it safely.

Why: Phase 3 serves this file. It must load on its own and say which model it is.

If skipped: The API would have nothing to serve.

docs.title: What Is Saved?
docs.text:
One Python dictionary, written with joblib.dump:

  • pipeline: the fitted scaler and model.
  • feature_names: the two input column names, in order.
  • model_version: the model.version setting (v1.0).
  • scikit_learn_version: the installed version at training time (1.9.1). The API compares it with its own, because a saved model may fail to load, or answer differently, under another version.
  • train_start_season and train_end_season: 2020 and 2024.
def save_model(pipeline, config: dict, start_season: int, train_end_season: int) -> Path:
    """Write the fitted pipeline beside the facts needed to load it later."""
    output = resolve_path(config["model"]["output_path"])
    output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    bundle = {
        "pipeline": pipeline,
        "feature_names": INPUT_COLUMNS,
        "model_version": config["model"]["version"],
        "scikit_learn_version": sklearn.__version__,
        "train_start_season": int(start_season),
        "train_end_season": int(train_end_season),
    }
    # Write beside the real file and swap only after the write finishes, so a failed run
    # cannot leave a half-written model in place of a good one.
    partial = output.with_name(output.name + ".partial")
    try:
        joblib.dump(bundle, partial)
        os.replace(partial, output)
    except Exception:
        partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise
    return output
  • Size: 1,902 bytes, so it is small enough to copy into the Docker image.
  • Round trip: the saved file loads with the six keys above, and a fresh fit gives the same probabilities as the loaded pipeline.
  • A failed save keeps the old file. If the write fails, the half-written .partial file is removed and the earlier model is left as it was.
  • The file extension .joblib is a convention. joblib writes to any file name.
  • Local only: models/, mlflow.db, and mlartifacts/ are in .gitignore, so the saved model and the MLflow records are not committed. results/run-summary.json is committed, and it is the readable record of the latest run.

docs.title: What Is the Run Summary File?
docs.text:
Each training run also writes results/run-summary.json, a small readable record of the run. A reader can open it without MLflow and without loading the saved model.

  • What it holds: the settings, the scikit-learn version, the data file and its fingerprint, the scores for each group, and the values the model learned.
  • Learned values: the scaler's averages and spreads, the two weights, and the intercept. They let a reader check a prediction by hand: standardize each input with the average and spread, multiply by its weight, add the intercept, and pass the total through the logistic function.
  • Committed to git. The file is overwritten on every run, so it always describes the latest run, and MLflow keeps the full history on your machine.
  • Stable on purpose. It has no run ID, no timestamp, no git commit, and no machine paths, because each of those changes on every run or commit. Decimals are rounded to 6 places. A rerun with the same settings and data writes the identical bytes, so the file shows a change in git only when something real changed.
  • Written safely. It is written to a .partial file and swapped into place, like the model file.
    # Rounding to six places keeps this file identical when the run itself did not change.
    text = json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n"
    output = resolve_path(config["tracking"]["summary_path"])
    output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    partial = output.with_name(output.name + ".partial")
    try:
        partial.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        os.replace(partial, output)
    except Exception:
        partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise

docs.title: Reading the Differences
docs.text:
• model.joblib is the model itself. It is the only file the API needs. It does not say how well the model scored.
  • mlflow.db is the logbook. It records what each run used and scored, and it points to the run's files. It holds numbers and text only. If you delete it, the model and files stay, but MLflow can no longer list the runs.
  • mlartifacts/ is the shelf of files. The logbook (mlflow.db) says which run a file belongs to, and mlartifacts/ holds the file. The two are only useful together, so keep or delete them as a pair.
  • run-summary.json is the committed receipt. It repeats the key facts of the latest run in a form git can compare line by line. The database and the shelf cannot be compared that way, because they are binary or hold run ids and times.

docs.title: What Is Inside mlartifacts/?
docs.text:
mlartifacts/
  <run id>/artifacts/            files in the run's own file list
    model/model.joblib             copy of the working model
    plots/confusion_matrix_validation.png
    config/config.yaml             copy of the settings used
  models/m-<id>/artifacts/       the MLflow-format model (a logged model)
    MLmodel                        description of the model
    model.skops                    the model, in skops format
    conda.yaml, python_env.yaml    the environment it needs
    requirements.txt               the packages it needs
  • Two copies of the model. model.joblib is plain and carries the extra facts the API checks. The MLflow-format copy lets MLflow's own tools load the model in one call. Both come from the same fitted model. See Why Is the Model Stored Twice?.
  • joblib and skops are two ways to write a model to disk. joblib is the general way and works on any Python object. skops is the format MLflow's scikit-learn support uses.
  • Where the settings go. config/config.yaml is the input. The copy under mlartifacts/ is a snapshot of what was used for that run.
  • Why they are not committed. The database is binary and changes on every run, it records an absolute path on one machine, and one command rebuilds both. See Decisions.
  • Terms. The Glossary defines artifact, artifact store, logged model, and SQLite.

docs.title: What Was Checked?
docs.text:
• A copy of the project containing only config/, data/, src/, and results/ (no mlflow.db, mlartifacts/, or models/), with results/run-summary.json deleted first. Running python -m src.model.train printed the eight lines above and rewrote the summary file identically to the committed one (SUMMARY_IDENTICAL: True from a byte comparison).

docs.title: What Is Not Guaranteed?
docs.text:
• Other machines. The check ran on one Mac with Python 3.13.14. A different operating system or processor could change a decimal beyond the 6th place, which rounding hides most of the time but not always.
  • Other package versions. The pins make a match likely. A different scikit-learn can change the weights, and the summary file records scikit_learn_version so you can see it.
  • A fresh download. See the Path B heads-up above.
  • The recorded git commit. MLflow tags each run with the commit that was checked out at the time. It is not in the summary file, so it does not affect the comparison.
  • Phases 3 to 5. This page covers the model only. The API, containers, and web app are planned in Remaining Phases.

docs.text:
Status: Built and tested. All 7 steps are done, and pytest passes 47 tests (30 from earlier phases and 17 new). Needs first: Phase 2, which is built. Its output is the saved model models/model.joblib. If that file is missing, run python -m src.model.train first.

Phase 3 wraps the trained model in a small web service that runs on your own computer. A person (or a program) sends the two model inputs as JSON, and the service returns the predicted winner and the home win probability as JSON. Nothing in this phase touches AWS or Docker. Those come later, starting with Phase 4.

To run it, activate the virtual environment and start the service. The Implementation page has the full run guide, with curl examples and the real output of each.

    F -->|"loaded once at start-up"| D

docs.title: Steps in Order
docs.text:
• Step 1. Load the saved model once, when the service starts. Read models/model.joblib (the path comes from model.output_path in config/config.yaml). Compare the scikit-learn version saved inside the file with the installed one, and stop with a clear message if they differ.
  • Step 2. Define the request and the response. The request holds two decimal numbers. The response holds the prediction and the probability.
  • Step 3. Add the POST /predict route. Put the two numbers in a NumPy array in the saved input order, and return the model's answer.
  • Step 4. Add the GET /health route. It reports that the service is up and which model version it loaded.
  • Step 5. Reject bad input with a clear error. A missing field, an extra field, a value that is not a number, or a number far outside the possible range returns status 422 with an error that names the problem.
  • Step 6. Write tests that call both routes with made-up data and no saved model file.
  • Step 7. Run it locally and test it with curl. Start the service with a one-line command, and send the worked example from the model page.

docs.title: Details in Brief
docs.text:
• One route to predict. POST /predict takes JSON like {"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}. Both fields are required.
  • The response has four fields:
    • prediction: 1 for a home win, 0 for an away win.
    • predicted_label: the same answer as text.
    • home_win_probability: the model's chance (0 to 1) that the home team wins.
    • model_version: the model.version setting saved in the file, for example v1.0.
  • The pick rule is the same as scoring. A probability above 0.5 is a home win, and exactly 0.5 is an away win. See Part 2.
  • Worked example. The inputs -0.5 and -18.0 (game 2025_07_NE_TEN) return a home win probability of 0.3296 and the prediction 0, which matches the model's own output in Part 2.
  • Valid ranges: win percentage difference from -1 to 1, which is the full possible range. Point margin difference from -100 to 100, which is a loose guard, because the real data runs about -49 to 39.
  • Unknown fields are rejected, so a misspelled name fails loudly and is not ignored.
  • The scaler is inside the model file, so the API sends raw inputs. The API never standardizes anything itself.
  • FastAPI, not Flask. Both can serve this model. FastAPI does the input checks (missing field, extra field, wrong type, out-of-range number) from one request definition, and it gives a test page at /docs with no extra code. In Flask, those checks would be written by hand. FastAPI also pairs with the Mangum adapter already pinned for Lambda in Phase 4, while Flask would need a different adapter. Flask is a little shorter for a route with no checks, which is the one place it is simpler.
  • No cloud code yet. The adapter that lets AWS Lambda run the same app (Mangum) is added in Phase 4. See What Is Mangum?.
  • Built so Lambda can reuse it. Phase 4 runs this same app in Lambda, so Phase 3 keeps four things true:
    • The app is one object named app, importable from the module src/api/app.py, with no code that reads the command line when it is imported.
    • The model loads in the app's start-up step through the load_model function, not inside a route. Phase 4 reuses load_model on Lambda and calls it once, on the first call.
    • Every file path goes through resolve_path in src/config.py, which finds the project folder from the code's own location. The Lambda zip keeps the same folder layout (src/, config/, models/), so the same paths work there.
    • Tests call the app in memory (FastAPI's test client), so they need no server and no network.
  • NumPy, not pandas, in the API. The Lambda zip fits under its size limit only without pandas (231.3 MB without it, 278.4 MB with it). So the API files must not import pandas, directly or through src/model/features.py, which imports it. The API reads the input names from the saved model file, passes the two numbers to the model as a plain numpy array in that order, and silences the one expected scikit-learn warning about column names. A test reads the API files and checks that none of them imports pandas. See the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • Packages: fastapi, uvicorn, and pydantic are already pinned in requirements.txt. uvicorn is the program that runs the service on your machine, and pydantic checks that each request has the right fields. See the Glossary for both.

docs.title: Phase 3 Implementation: Local Prediction API
docs.text:
This page explains how the Phase 3 service works and how to run it on your own computer. The service takes two numbers about a game and returns the model's pick and the home team's chance of winning, as JSON. For the short version, see the Brief.

Status: built and tested. The code is in src/api/app.py and src/api/schemas.py, and the tests are in tests/test_api.py. Every request and response shown below was produced by the running service. The full test suite passes with 47 tests: the 30 from earlier phases and 17 new ones.

docs.title: How Do I Run It Locally?
What Is Needed First?
docs.text:
Need How to check or get it Python 3.13 and the project's virtual environment See the run environment. The pinned packages pip install -r requirements.txt The saved model models/model.joblib python -m src.model.train. The file is not committed, so a fresh checkout needs this step.

No AWS account, no internet connection, and no Docker are needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Project and Activate the Environment
docs.text:
From the project folder, activate the virtual environment so that python is the project's Python:

source .venv/bin/activate

Install the packages if this is a new checkout:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Train the model if models/model.joblib does not exist:

python -m src.model.train

docs.title: Step 2: Start the Service
docs.text:
python -m uvicorn src.api.app:app --port 8000

uvicorn is the program that runs the service. See What Is uvicorn? below. Starting it with python -m makes sure the one in the project's environment is used, even if the shell cannot find a bare uvicorn command.

When the service is ready, the terminal prints these lines and then waits:

INFO:     Started server process [32104]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
  • The terminal stays busy. The service runs until you stop it. Open a second terminal for the curl commands below.
  • Only this computer can reach it. The address 127.0.0.1 means "this machine", so nobody else on your network can connect.
  • Each request is logged in that terminal, for example POST /predict HTTP/1.1" 200 OK.
  • Port already in use? If the terminal says address already in use, another program owns port 8000. mkdocs serve uses port 8000 by default. Either stop that program, or start this service on another port, such as --port 8001, and use that port in every command below.

docs.title: Step 3: Check That It Is Running
docs.text:
In the second terminal:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

{"status":"ok","model_version":"v1.0","scikit_learn_version":"1.9.1"}

docs.title: Step 4: Stop the Service
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C in the terminal where it is running. It prints Shutting down and exits.

docs.title: How Do I Ask for a Prediction?
What Are the Two Numbers?
docs.text:
The model uses two numbers, both measured before the game from the games already played earlier in the same season. Each one is the home team's value minus the away team's value.

Field How to work it out Allowed range win_pct_differential Home team win percentage minus away team win percentage. A 6-2 team is 0.75, and a 4-4 team is 0.50, so the difference is 0.25. -1 to 1 point_diff_per_game_differential Home team points scored minus points allowed per game, minus the same figure for the away team. A team that is +8.0 per game against a team that is -2.0 per game gives 10.0. -100 to 100
  • A positive number favors the home team.
  • Week 1: no team has played yet, so both numbers are 0.
  • Whole numbers are fine, for example 0 and 5. Numbers written as text, such as "0.5", are rejected.
  • The range for the second field is a loose guard. The real data runs from about -49 to 39.
  • The inputs are explained further in Phase 2 Part 1.

docs.title: Example 1: A Game Where the Away Team Is Stronger
docs.text:
This is game 2025_07_NE_TEN: the home team (Tennessee) is weaker on both numbers.

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}'

{"prediction":0,"predicted_label":"away win","home_win_probability":0.3296,"model_version":"v1.0"}

The model gives the home team a 32.96% chance, which is below 50%, so the pick is an away win. New England won this game, so the pick was correct. This is the same game worked by hand in Part 2.

What the pieces of the command mean:

Part What it does -X POST Sends a POST request, which is what /predict accepts. -H "Content-Type: application/json" Tells the service that the body is JSON. -d '{...}' The body: the two numbers, as JSON. Single quotes outside, double quotes inside. http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict This computer, port 8000, the /predict route.

docs.title: Example 2: Two Evenly Matched Teams
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": 0, "point_diff_per_game_differential": 0}'

{"prediction":1,"predicted_label":"home win","home_win_probability":0.5364,"model_version":"v1.0"}

With no difference between the teams, the model still gives the home team a 53.64% chance. This is the home-field edge the model learned. See Part 2.

docs.title: Example 3: The Home Team Is Stronger
docs.text:
A home team that is 6-2 against a 4-4 away team (0.25), and +10.0 points per game better:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": 0.25, "point_diff_per_game_differential": 10.0}'

{"prediction":1,"predicted_label":"home win","home_win_probability":0.6467,"model_version":"v1.0"}

The model gives the home team a 64.67% chance, and the pick is a home win.

docs.title: Showing the Status Code
docs.text:
Add -w to print the HTTP status code after the body, and -s to hide curl's progress meter:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}'

{"prediction":0,"predicted_label":"away win","home_win_probability":0.3296,"model_version":"v1.0"}
HTTP 200

To print the JSON on several lines, pipe it through Python's formatter. This is one command with two parts, so it stays in one block:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}' | python -m json.tool

docs.title: What Is in the Response?
docs.text: Field Type What it means prediction whole number, 1 or 0 1 is a home win and 0 is an away win. A probability above 0.5 gives 1, and exactly 0.5 gives 0, the same rule as scoring in Part 2. predicted_label text The same pick in words: home win or away win. home_win_probability decimal number, 0 to 1 The model's chance that the home team wins, rounded to 4 places. The pick is made from the unrounded value. model_version text The model.version setting that was saved with the model (v1.0).

docs.title: What Happens With Bad Input?
docs.text: A request that fails a check gets status 422 and a JSON error that names the problem. The model is never called. Each example below was sent to the running service.

docs.title: Reading an Error
docs.text:
{"detail":[{"type":"less_than_equal","loc":["body","win_pct_differential"],"msg":"Input should be less than or equal to 1","input":1.5,"ctx":{"le":1.0}}]}
Part What it tells you detail A list with one entry for each problem. A request with two problems has two entries. type A short code for the kind of problem. loc Where the problem is: body, then the field name. msg A plain sentence about the problem. input The value that was sent. ctx Extra detail, such as the limit that was exceeded.

docs.title: Error Examples
docs.text:
A value out of range, and a missing field. This one request has two problems:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": 1.5}'

{"detail":[{"type":"less_than_equal","loc":["body","win_pct_differential"],"msg":"Input should be less than or equal to 1","input":1.5,"ctx":{"le":1.0}},{"type":"missing","loc":["body","point_diff_per_game_differential"],"msg":"Field required","input":{"win_pct_differential":1.5}}]}
HTTP 422

An extra field. A misspelled or unknown name is refused, not ignored:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": 0.1, "point_diff_per_game_differential": 1.0, "week": 3}'

{"detail":[{"type":"extra_forbidden","loc":["body","week"],"msg":"Extra inputs are not permitted","input":3}]}
HTTP 422

A number written as text:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": "0.5", "point_diff_per_game_differential": 1.0}'

{"detail":[{"type":"float_type","loc":["body","win_pct_differential"],"msg":"Input should be a valid number","input":"0.5"}]}
HTTP 422

Not a number (NaN): standard JSON has no NaN, but some tools write it. It is refused:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"win_pct_differential": NaN, "point_diff_per_game_differential": 1.0}'

{"detail":[{"type":"finite_number","loc":["body","win_pct_differential"],"msg":"Input should be a finite number","input":"NaN"}]}
HTTP 422

The input shows "NaN" as text. FastAPI cannot write a real NaN into a JSON response, so the service has its own error handler that swaps it for the string. See Step 5.

A body that is not JSON:

curl -s -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d 'not json'

{"detail":[{"type":"json_invalid","loc":["body",0],"msg":"JSON decode error","input":{},"ctx":{"error":"Expecting value"}}]}
HTTP 422

docs.title: Summary of Rejections
docs.text: Request problem Status type in the error A field is missing 422 missing An unknown field is added 422 extra_forbidden A value is text, or a true/false 422 float_type A value is outside its range 422 less_than_equal or greater_than_equal A value is NaN or infinity 422 finite_number The body is not valid JSON 422 json_invalid

docs.title: How Can I Try It in a Browser?
docs.text:
FastAPI serves a test page, so no curl is needed. With the service running, open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs.

  1. Click POST /predict to open it.
  2. Click Try it out.
  3. Edit the JSON in the box. It starts with an example of the right shape.
  4. Click Execute. The page shows the status code and the response body, and the curl command it sent.

The same page lists GET /health, and shows the field descriptions and the allowed ranges. The machine-readable description of the service is at http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json. Both pages returned status 200.

docs.title: What Is uvicorn?
docs.text:
A FastAPI app is only a Python object. It does not listen for requests by itself, so something has to run it. uvicorn is that program (a web server). It opens a port on your computer, receives each HTTP request, passes it to the app, and sends the app's answer back to the caller. The two talk through ASGI, the standard interface between Python web servers and web apps. See the Glossary for the short definition, and the uvicorn documentation for its options.

  • Only for the laptop. uvicorn runs the service in Phase 3. On AWS Lambda there is no port to listen on, so it is not used there and is left out of the Lambda zip. Mangum takes its place. See What Is Mangum?.
  • It is not part of the API's logic. The routes, the input checks, and the model call are all in the FastAPI app. Swapping uvicorn for another server would not change an answer.
Part of the command What it means python -m uvicorn Run the uvicorn installed in the active environment. src.api.app:app Import the module src/api/app.py and run the object named app inside it. The part before the colon is the file, and the part after is the variable. --port 8000 Listen on port 8000. With no --host, it listens only on this computer.

docs.title: How Does It Start?
docs.text:
The model file is read once, in the app's start-up step, and kept in memory. Every request after that reuses it.

flowchart TB

    B --> C{"models/model.joblib<br/>exists?"}
    C -->|"no"| X1["Stop with a message:<br/>run python -m src.model.train"]
    C -->|"yes"| D["Load the saved file"]
    D --> E{"File readable, with the<br/>four required keys?"}
    E -->|"no"| X3["Stop with a message that<br/>names the problem"]
    E -->|"yes"| F{"Saved scikit-learn version<br/>equals the installed one?"}
    F -->|"no"| X2["Stop with a message that<br/>names both versions"]
    F -->|"yes"| H{"Saved input names match<br/>the two request fields?"}
    H -->|"no"| X4["Stop with a message that<br/>names the input names"]
    H -->|"yes"| G["Ready for requests"]

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller (curl)
    participant A as FastAPI app
    participant V as Input check
    participant M as Model in memory
    C->>A: POST /predict with JSON
    A->>V: check fields, types, ranges
    alt input is not valid

    else input is valid

docs.title: Which Files Were Added?
docs.text:
File What it holds src/api/app.py The app object, create_app, the start-up step (load_model), the 0.5 rule (label_for), and the two routes. src/api/schemas.py The three JSON shapes: PredictRequest, PredictResponse, and HealthResponse. tests/test_api.py 17 tests for both routes, the start-up checks, and the no-pandas rule. requirements.txt One new pinned line, httpx2==2.16.2, used only by the tests.
  • No new settings. The service reuses model.output_path from config/config.yaml. The host and port are given on the command line.
  • httpx2 is test-only. FastAPI's test client calls the app through it, and the installed Starlette asks for httpx2 and prints a warning with the older httpx. It is not needed in the Lambda zip. It brought in two helper packages, httpcore2 and truststore, which are left unpinned like the project's other indirect packages.
  • No __init__.py files, matching the rest of the project.

docs.title: Step 1: Load the Saved Model at Start-Up
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Read models/model.joblib once, check it, and keep it in memory.

Why: Loading on every request would be slow, and a model saved by a different scikit-learn version may fail to load or answer differently. Failing at start-up is clearer than failing on the first request.

If skipped: A missing or mismatched model would show up as an error in the middle of a request.

  • Where the path comes from: model.output_path in config/config.yaml, turned into a full path with resolve_path from src/config.py. That function finds the project folder from the code's own location, so the same path works from any folder, and in the Lambda zip in Phase 4.
  • What is in the file: a dictionary with pipeline, feature_names, model_version, scikit_learn_version, train_start_season, and train_end_season. See Step 7 of Phase 2.
  • Where the model lives: in the app's start-up step (FastAPI's lifespan), stored on app.state. The routes read it from there. Importing src/api/app.py builds the app but does not read the file.
  • Why start-up and not import time: the tests build the app without a real model file, and Lambda (in Phase 4) reuses the same load_model function. Mangum would run this start-up step on every request by default, so Phase 4 turns that off and calls load_model itself, once, on the first call. See What Is Mangum?.
  • Checks, in this order: the file exists, it loads, it holds the four keys the API needs (pipeline, feature_names, model_version, scikit_learn_version), the scikit-learn version matches, and the saved input names match the request fields.

If any check fails, the service refuses to start, and uvicorn prints a traceback that ends with one of these messages (the RuntimeError line):

Problem Message The file is missing No saved model at models/model.joblib. Run python -m src.model.train first. The file cannot be read, or is not a dictionary, or lacks a key Could not read the saved model at models/model.joblib: <reason>. Run python -m src.model.train to rebuild it. Saved scikit-learn version differs Saved model was built with scikit-learn <saved> but <installed> is installed. Retrain with python -m src.model.train, or install scikit-learn==<saved>. The saved input names are not the two request fields Could not read the saved model at models/model.joblib: input names [...] do not match the API fields.

The real output when the model file is missing ends like this, and the process exits with code 3:

RuntimeError: No saved model at models/model.joblib. Run python -m src.model.train first.

ERROR:    Application startup failed. Exiting.

docs.title: Step 2: Define the Request and the Response
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Describe the exact JSON the service accepts and returns, in one place.

Why: One definition gives the input checks, the error messages, and the /docs test page together.

If skipped: The checks would be written by hand in each route.

The request, from src/api/schemas.py:

class PredictRequest(BaseModel):
    """The two pre-game numbers. Extra fields are refused so a typo is not ignored."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

    win_pct_differential: float = Field(ge=-1, le=1, allow_inf_nan=False, ...)
    # A loose guard, because the real data runs about -49 to 39.
    point_diff_per_game_differential: float = Field(ge=-100, le=100, allow_inf_nan=False, ...)
  • extra="forbid" refuses unknown fields.
  • strict=True refuses numbers written as text, and true or false, in place of numbers. Whole numbers such as 0 are still accepted.
  • allow_inf_nan=False refuses NaN and infinity.
  • The field names match the model's input names (INPUT_COLUMNS in src/model/features.py), but the API does not import that file. At start-up it checks that the names saved in the model file are the same as the two request fields.

The response has four fields (prediction, predicted_label, home_win_probability, model_version), described in What Is in the Response?. The health response has three (status, model_version, scikit_learn_version).

docs.title: Step 3: Add the POST /predict Route
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Turn a valid request into a prediction.

Why: This is the route the web app calls.

If skipped: There would be no way to ask the model a question.

@app.post("/predict", response_model=PredictResponse, summary="Predict which team wins.")
def predict(request: PredictRequest) -> PredictResponse:
    """Score one game from the two numbers, in the order saved with the model."""
    saved = app.state.model
    row = np.array([[getattr(request, name) for name in saved["feature_names"]]], dtype=float)
    # The scaler was fitted on a table with column names, and this call passes a plain array
    # so the service does not import pandas. The probability is the same either way.
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message=r"X does not have valid feature names", category=UserWarning)
        probability = float(saved["pipeline"].predict_proba(row)[0, 1])
    prediction, predicted_label = label_for(probability)
    return PredictResponse(
        prediction=prediction,
        predicted_label=predicted_label,
        home_win_probability=round(probability, 4),
        model_version=saved["model_version"],
    )
  1. FastAPI checks the request against PredictRequest before the route code runs.
  2. The route looks up each saved input name on the request and builds a numpy array with one row and two columns, in the order of feature_names from the model file. The order of the fields in the JSON does not matter.
  3. The route calls predict_proba and takes the probability of class 1 (a home win).
  4. label_for applies the 0.5 rule: above 0.5 is (1, "home win"), and anything else, including exactly 0.5, is (0, "away win"). It is applied to the unrounded probability.
  5. The response rounds the probability to 4 places.

docs.title: Why Does the API Use NumPy Instead of pandas?
docs.text:
The API uses NumPy only. It does not use pandas, although training and cleaning do. The two numbers go to the model as a NumPy array and not as a pandas table (a DataFrame).

  • The Lambda zip fits only without pandas. It is 231.3 MB without it and 278.4 MB with it, against a 250 MB limit. See the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • src/model/features.py imports pandas at the top, so no file in src/api/ may import from it. The input names come from the model file instead.
  • One warning is expected. The scaler was fitted on a table with column names, so a plain array makes scikit-learn warn that "X does not have valid feature names". The probability is the same. The route silences this one warning and no others.
  • The answer is unchanged. With only NumPy installed, the inputs -0.5 and -18.0 give 0.3296, matching Part 2.

docs.title: Step 4: Add the GET /health Route
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Report that the service is running and which model it loaded.

Why: It is the quickest way to check a running service, and it shows which model version is answering.

If skipped: A person could not tell a running service from a stopped one without sending a real prediction.

The response is {"status":"ok","model_version":"v1.0","scikit_learn_version":"1.9.1"}. The route reads only from memory. It does not open the file or call the model. The scikit_learn_version is the one saved in the model file, and start-up has already checked that it equals the installed one.

docs.title: Step 5: Reject Bad Input Clearly
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Make every bad request return an error that names the problem, and never a prediction or a crash.

Why: The web app and a person with curl both need to see what to fix.

If skipped: A bad value could reach the model and return a meaningless probability.

flowchart TB
    A["Request arrives"] --> B{"Valid JSON?"}
    B -->|"no"| E["422: json_invalid"]
    B -->|"yes"| C{"Both fields present,<br/>no extra fields?"}
    C -->|"no"| E2["422: missing or extra_forbidden"]
    C -->|"yes"| D{"Both are numbers<br/>inside their ranges?"}
    D -->|"no"| E3["422: float_type, finite_number,<br/>or a range error"]
    D -->|"yes"| F["Run the model"]

The checks all come from the request definition in Step 2, and FastAPI answers a failed check with status 422. One piece of extra code was needed. When a value is NaN, the error body would contain a real NaN, which JSON cannot hold, and FastAPI crashed while writing the 422. The service has its own handler for these errors (reject_invalid_request in src/api/app.py) that replaces a non-finite number with the text "NaN" or "Infinity" and then sends the 422. Real examples are shown in Error Examples.

docs.title: Step 6: Run the Tests
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Check both routes, the start-up checks, and the no-pandas rule, without a real saved model or the internet.

Why: The tests keep the Lambda size result and the input rules from breaking later.

If skipped: A change could pass unnoticed until the deployed function failed.

python -m pytest

Expected: 47 passed, with no warnings, in about 11 seconds. Without models/model.joblib, test 17 is skipped instead, and 46 pass.

  • Made-up model. A fixture fits a tiny pipeline on 40 made-up rows (fixed random seed), saves it in the same dictionary format that training writes, and points the service at it. The tests never touch models/model.joblib, except test 17.
  • In-memory calls. FastAPI's test client calls the app without starting a server. It is used as a context manager (with TestClient(app)), because that is what runs the start-up step.
# Test What it checks 1 test_prediction_matches_the_pipeline The probability from /predict equals the pipeline's own answer, rounded to 4 places. 2 test_pick_rule label_for gives an away win for 0.0, 0.4999, and exactly 0.5, and a home win for 0.5001 and 1.0. 3 test_response_fields The response has the four fields with the right types, and whole-number inputs are accepted. 4 test_field_order_does_not_change_the_answer The same two values with the JSON fields in the opposite order give the same response. 5 test_missing_field_is_rejected Status 422, and the error names the missing field. 6 test_extra_field_is_rejected Status 422, and the error names the extra field. 7 test_text_value_is_rejected Both "abc" and "0.5" give 422. 8 test_out_of_range_value_is_rejected 1.5 and 500 are rejected and name the field, and the edge values 1 and -100 are accepted. 9 test_not_a_number_is_rejected A body containing NaN gives 422. 10 test_invalid_json_is_rejected A body that is not valid JSON gives 422. 11 test_health Status 200, with the three expected fields. 12 test_missing_model_file_stops_startup Start-up raises an error that says to run the training command. 13 test_unreadable_model_file_stops_startup A file holding plain text stops start-up with "Could not read the saved model". 14 test_version_mismatch_stops_startup A saved scikit-learn version of 0.0.0 stops start-up and names both versions. 15 test_wrong_feature_names_stop_startup Saved input names that are not the two request fields stop start-up. 16 test_api_files_do_not_import_pandas The API files are read as text and checked: none imports pandas, mlflow, matplotlib, or anything from src/model/. Checking sys.modules would not work, because scikit-learn loads pandas on its own when it is installed. 17 test_real_model_worked_example With the real model, the inputs -0.5 and -18.0 return the exact response shown in Example 1. Skipped if models/model.joblib does not exist.

docs.title: What If Something Goes Wrong?
docs.text: What you see Likely cause What to do command not found: uvicorn The virtual environment is not active, or the shell has no uvicorn command. Run source .venv/bin/activate, and start the service with python -m uvicorn .... address already in use Another program, often mkdocs serve, owns port 8000. Stop it, or use --port 8001 here and in every curl command. RuntimeError: No saved model at models/model.joblib The model has not been trained on this machine. Run python -m src.model.train. RuntimeError: Saved model was built with scikit-learn ... The installed scikit-learn differs from the one that trained the model. Run pip install -r requirements.txt, or retrain. curl: (7) Failed to connect The service is not running, or is on another port. Check the first terminal, and check the port in the command. Status 422 The request failed an input check. Read loc and msg in the error. See Reading an Error. Status 404 The path is wrong. The routes are /predict and /health. /predict needs POST. Status 405 GET was sent to /predict. Add -X POST and a body.

docs.title: What Carries Into Phase 4?
docs.text:
• The same app object is wrapped by Mangum in Phase 4, so the local tests cover the code that runs on Lambda.
  • The no-pandas rule keeps the Lambda zip under its size limit.
  • The load_model function is reused on Lambda. Mangum runs the app's start-up step on every request by default, so Phase 4 turns that off and loads the model once, on the first call, instead.
  • The folder layout (src/, config/, models/) must stay the same inside the zip, so resolve_path finds the same files.

docs.title: Phase 4 Brief: AWS Deployment
docs.text:
Status: Built and tested. All 11 steps are done, and pytest passes 53 tests. The API is live at https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. Needs first: Phase 3, which is built, and a trained model at models/model.joblib. Also an AWS account, AWS CLI version 2, and credentials on the machine, as listed in the run environment.

Phase 4 puts the Phase 3 API on the internet. The same FastAPI app runs inside an AWS Lambda function, and an API Gateway address in front of it gives the world a public URL for POST /predict and GET /health. The worked example sent to that URL returns the same answer as the local service (0.3296), and all 1,759 games give the same answers as the local model. The web app that calls it comes in Phase 5.

docs.title: How Do the Pieces Fit Together?
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Caller<br/>(curl, or the web app<br/>in Phase 5)"] -->|"HTTPS request"| B["API Gateway<br/>HTTP API<br/>routes and CORS"]
    B -->|"Lambda event"| C
    subgraph L["AWS Lambda function (zip, arm64, Python 3.13)"]
        C["Mangum"] --> D["FastAPI app<br/>(same code as Phase 3)"]
        D --> E["Saved model<br/>loaded once, on the first call"]
    end
    L -.->|"logs"| F["CloudWatch Logs"]
  • API Gateway receives the request, applies the CORS rules, and calls the function.
  • Mangum translates between the event Lambda hands the function and the request FastAPI expects. See What Is Mangum?.
  • The FastAPI app and the model are the Phase 3 code, so the local tests cover what runs on AWS.

docs.title: Steps in Order
docs.text:
• Step 1. Add the Lambda entry point. A new file (src/api/lambda_handler.py) wraps the app with Mangum. Mangum runs the app's start-up step on every request by default, which would re-read the model each time, so the entry point turns that off and loads the model itself on the first call.
  • Step 2. Test the entry point with no AWS. Call handler with a made-up API Gateway HTTP API event for POST /predict. The worked example returns status 200 and a home win probability of 0.3296.
  • Step 3. Measure the package size first. The serving packages for Linux, arm64, and Python 3.13 come to 231.3 MB unzipped without pandas, under the 250 MB limit, so the zip route works. See the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • Step 4. Build the zip. It holds the installed serving packages, src/, config/config.yaml, and models/model.joblib, in the same folder layout as the project so every path still resolves. It is 231,252,596 bytes unzipped and 63,452,500 bytes zipped.
  • Step 5. Create the function. Python 3.13, arm64, 1769 MB, a 10-second timeout, one environment variable, and a role that can only write logs.
  • Step 6. Test the function in AWS with the same made-up event as Step 2.
  • Step 7. Create the API Gateway HTTP API with the routes POST /predict and GET /health, both pointing at the function.
  • Step 8. Set CORS on the gateway. It allows the local web app address. The CloudFront address is added once it exists (Phase 5).
  • Step 9. Check the public address with curl and the worked example. It returns the same 0.3296 as the local API.
  • Step 10. Check the deployed model against the local model. All 1,759 games give the same pick and the same probability, and the accuracy equals the run summary.
  • Step 11. Write the deployment steps down, so they can be repeated by hand. See Deployment Guide.

docs.title: Details in Brief
docs.text:
• Lambda runs from a zip file, not a container image, so no Docker and no ECR are needed for this phase. The reasons are in Decisions.
  • Serving packages only. The zip uses a shorter list than requirements.txt, in requirements-serve.txt: scikit-learn, numpy, joblib, PyYAML, fastapi, pydantic, and mangum, plus scipy, which scikit-learn brings in and which is not pinned today. It leaves out pandas, mlflow, matplotlib, boto3, uvicorn, and the test packages. Lambda already provides boto3, and uvicorn is replaced by Mangum.
  • Built for the function's platform, not the Mac's. The packages are installed as Linux arm64 for Python 3.13, the same chip type and Python version the function uses. The command and what each flag does are in the Phase 4 Implementation, Step 3.
  • The model is copied into the zip at build time. It is not committed to git and is not downloaded at start-up. The saved scikit-learn version must equal the one in the zip (1.9.1), or the service refuses to start, as in Phase 3.
  • The zip is larger than the console's upload limit. It is 63.2 MB zipped, and the console accepts about 50 MB, so the zip was uploaded through S3 (a temporary deploy/ key in the data bucket, deleted afterward).
  • The function role can only write logs. Each AWS identity gets only the access its job needs.
  • The API is public, with no key. A key in a browser app would be visible to every visitor, so it would not protect anything. There are no protection rules, request limit, or firewall for now.
  • Function settings: 1769 MB of memory, a 10-second timeout, and one environment variable, JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING=0, which stops a harmless joblib warning. Logs are kept for 14 days. Accuracy is the only priority, so memory is not tuned further. The measurements are in Phase 4 Implementation, Step 5.
  • Deployment is a set of written steps (commands that can be repeated by hand), with no deploy.yml workflow. They are on Deployment Guide.
  • Settings: none new in config/config.yaml. The Lambda settings live in the deployment steps.

docs.title: What If the Zip Is Too Large?
docs.text:
scikit-learn, scipy, and numpy are large, so the zip could have gone over Lambda's 250 MB unzipped limit. Step 3 found out before anything else was built: the zip fits (231.3 MB unzipped) as long as pandas is left out. This fall-back stays unused unless the package grows past the limit. In that case, build one container image, store it in a private Amazon ECR repository, and run Lambda from that image. Docker is then needed earlier than Phase 6, for this one step.

flowchart TB
    A["Install serving packages<br/>for Linux arm64, Python 3.13"] --> B{"Unzipped size<br/>under 250 MB?"}
    B -->|"yes (231.3 MB measured)"| C["Build the zip<br/>and create the function"]
    B -->|"no"| D["Fall back: one container image<br/>in a private ECR repository"]
    C --> E["API Gateway routes<br/>and CORS point at the function"]
    D --> E

docs.title: What Could Go Wrong?
docs.text:
• A package that imports on a Mac can fail on Lambda, because the packages were downloaded for Linux. Steps 6, 9, and 10 are the proof, and the function ran with no import error.
  • The package has about 30.9 MB of room. A new large dependency, or a version bump, can push it over. Re-measure after changing a pin.
  • A public API can be called by anyone. For now there is no request limit and no firewall in front of it. That is acceptable for this project, and protection can be added later if it is needed.
  • CORS can block the browser. A wrong origin fails in the browser and not in curl, so the origin is checked again in Phase 5.

docs.title: Choices Made Along the Way
docs.text:
• Where the zip was staged. A temporary deploy/ key in the private data bucket, deleted once the function existed.
  • The serving package list. A separate pinned list, requirements-serve.txt, including scipy.
  • Memory. 1769 MB, and not a priority. See Decisions.
  • The other Phase 4 choices (zip or container image, no API key, written steps) are in Decisions.

docs.title: What Was Created
docs.text:
• Code: src/api/lambda_handler.py and six tests in tests/test_lambda_handler.py.
  • Packaging: requirements-serve.txt and the written build and deploy commands on Deployment Guide.
  • Settings: one new warning filter in pytest.ini, and none in config/config.yaml.
  • On AWS: one Lambda function, one function role (the identity Lambda requires the function to run as, which can only write logs), and one API Gateway HTTP API with two routes. All are in us-east-1.
  • Nothing committed that is generated. The zip and the build folder stay local, and build/ is already ignored by git.

docs.title: What Is Not in This Phase
docs.text:
• The web app and its hosting, in Phase 5.
  • Docker, in Phase 6. The README and the review come after it, in Phase 7 and Phase 8.
