docs.title: Phase 4 Deployment Guide
docs.text: This guide lists, in order, every command that built and deployed the Phase 4 API, and the commands that remove it again. Each step is explained in the Phase 4 Implementation.

docs.title: How Do the Sections Fit Together?
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Local["On this computer"]
        A["Build the Zip<br/>installed packages + project files"]
    end
    subgraph AWS["On AWS (us-east-1)"]
        B["Check the Account<br/>and that the names are free"] --> C["Create the Role<br/>logs only"]
        C --> D["Stage the Zip in S3<br/>and Create the Function"]
        D --> E["Create the HTTP API<br/>routes, permission, CORS"]
        E --> F["Check the public address"]
    end
    A --> B
    F --> G["Check the Deployed Model<br/>Against the Local Model"]
    G -.-> H["Remove Everything<br/>(written, not run)"]
  • Build the Zip runs on this computer and calls no AWS service.
  • Check the Account confirms the right account and that no resource with a name from this guide exists yet.
  • Create the Role, Stage the Zip and Create the Function, and Create the HTTP API create the AWS resources, in that order, because each needs the one before it.
  • Check the Deployed Model Against the Local Model proves the function runs the zip built here and gives the same answers as the local model.
  • Remove Everything deletes what this guide created. The commands are written and are not run as part of the deployment.

Run these from the project folder, in order. Resource names stay as written. <account-id>, <api-id>, and <integration-id> stand in for values that differ between accounts.

Why these settings: accuracy is the only requirement for this deployment. Latency and cost are not concerns. Memory is 1769 MB and may be changed if it helps, but it is not a priority. JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING=0 stops a harmless joblib warning about multiprocessing, which Lambda does not provide.

Before the first command:

  • AWS CLI 2.35.9 is installed, and the default credentials can reach the account that owns 510-m3-nfl-dataset in us-east-1.
  • The project virtual environment is Python 3.13.14.
  • models/model.joblib exists and was saved by scikit-learn 1.9.1.
  • requirements-serve.txt and src/api/lambda_handler.py exist.

docs.title: Build the Zip
docs.text:
1. Remove the previous build folder and zip.
rm -rf build/lambda build/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip
  1. Install the serving packages for Linux arm64 and Python 3.13.
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --target build/lambda --implementation cp --python-version 3.13 --platform manylinux_2_28_aarch64 --platform manylinux2014_aarch64 --only-binary=:all: --no-compile -r requirements-serve.txt
  1. Delete cached bytecode from the build.
find build/lambda -type d -name __pycache__ -prune -exec rm -rf {} +
  1. Copy the project files the function imports, keeping the folder layout.
mkdir -p build/lambda/src/api build/lambda/config build/lambda/models

cp src/config.py build/lambda/src/config.py

cp src/api/app.py src/api/lambda_handler.py src/api/schemas.py build/lambda/src/api/

cp config/config.yaml build/lambda/config/config.yaml

cp models/model.joblib build/lambda/models/model.joblib
  1. Zip the contents of build/lambda, so src/, config/, and models/ sit at the top.
(cd build/lambda && zip -r -q ../510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip .)

docs.title: Check the Account
docs.text:
1. Confirm the caller and the data bucket. The bucket command prints nothing when the bucket is reachable.
aws sts get-caller-identity --region us-east-1

aws s3api head-bucket --bucket 510-m3-nfl-dataset --region us-east-1
  1. Confirm the names are free. A missing function, role, or zip is the expected result. The API query should print 0.
aws lambda get-function --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --region us-east-1

aws iam get-role --role-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role --region us-east-1

aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --region us-east-1 --query "length(Items[?Name=='510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api'])" --output text

aws s3api head-object --bucket 510-m3-nfl-dataset --key deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip --region us-east-1

docs.title: Create the Role
docs.text:
1. Write the trust policy. It lets only Lambda assume the role. A statement id is omitted because IAM rejects a hyphenated id.
mkdir -p build

cat > build/trust-policy.json <<'EOF'
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com"},
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
EOF
  1. Create the role and attach the logs policy.
aws iam create-role --role-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role --assume-role-policy-document file://build/trust-policy.json --tags Key=project,Value=510-m3 --region us-east-1

aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole --region us-east-1

docs.title: Stage the Zip and Create the Function
docs.text:
1. Copy the zip into the data bucket.
aws s3 cp build/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip s3://510-m3-nfl-dataset/deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip --region us-east-1
  1. Create the function from that object. If this fails because the new role cannot be assumed yet, wait a few seconds and run it again, up to 5 times.
aws lambda create-function --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --runtime python3.13 --architectures arm64 --handler src.api.lambda_handler.handler --role arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role --code S3Bucket=510-m3-nfl-dataset,S3Key=deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip --memory-size 1769 --timeout 10 --environment "Variables={JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING=0}" --tags project=510-m3 --region us-east-1
  1. Wait until the function is active.
aws lambda wait function-active --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --region us-east-1
  1. Write the three test events. The predict event is the worked example. The health event has no body. The bad event sends only an out-of-range win percentage.
cat > build/predict-event.json <<'EOF'
{"version":"2.0","routeKey":"POST /predict","rawPath":"/predict","rawQueryString":"","headers":{"content-type":"application/json"},"requestContext":{"accountId":"123456789012","apiId":"test","domainName":"test.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com","http":{"method":"POST","path":"/predict","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","sourceIp":"127.0.0.1","userAgent":"test"},"requestId":"test","routeKey":"POST /predict","stage":"$default","time":"01/Jan/2026:00:00:00 +0000","timeEpoch":1767225600000},"body":"{\"win_pct_differential\": -0.5, \"point_diff_per_game_differential\": -18.0}","isBase64Encoded":false}
EOF

cat > build/health-event.json <<'EOF'
{"version":"2.0","routeKey":"GET /health","rawPath":"/health","rawQueryString":"","headers":{"content-type":"application/json"},"requestContext":{"accountId":"123456789012","apiId":"test","domainName":"test.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com","http":{"method":"GET","path":"/health","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","sourceIp":"127.0.0.1","userAgent":"test"},"requestId":"test","routeKey":"GET /health","stage":"$default","time":"01/Jan/2026:00:00:00 +0000","timeEpoch":1767225600000},"isBase64Encoded":false}
EOF

cat > build/bad-body-event.json <<'EOF'
{"version":"2.0","routeKey":"POST /predict","rawPath":"/predict","rawQueryString":"","headers":{"content-type":"application/json"},"requestContext":{"accountId":"123456789012","apiId":"test","domainName":"test.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com","http":{"method":"POST","path":"/predict","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","sourceIp":"127.0.0.1","userAgent":"test"},"requestId":"test","routeKey":"POST /predict","stage":"$default","time":"01/Jan/2026:00:00:00 +0000","timeEpoch":1767225600000},"body":"{\"win_pct_differential\": 1.5}","isBase64Encoded":false}
EOF
  1. Invoke the worked example twice, then health, then the bad body. Add --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out on AWS CLI version 2.
aws lambda invoke --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload file://build/predict-event.json --log-type Tail --region us-east-1 build/invoke-predict-1.json

aws lambda invoke --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload file://build/predict-event.json --log-type Tail --region us-east-1 build/invoke-predict-2.json

aws lambda invoke --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload file://build/health-event.json --log-type Tail --region us-east-1 build/invoke-health.json

aws lambda invoke --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload file://build/bad-body-event.json --log-type Tail --region us-east-1 build/invoke-bad.json
  1. Delete the staged zip and confirm the deploy/ prefix is empty.
aws s3 rm s3://510-m3-nfl-dataset/deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip --region us-east-1

aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket 510-m3-nfl-dataset --prefix deploy/ --region us-east-1

docs.title: Create the HTTP API
docs.text:
1. Create the API, one proxy integration, the two routes, and the $default stage.
aws apigatewayv2 create-api --name 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api --protocol-type HTTP --tags project=510-m3 --region us-east-1

aws apigatewayv2 create-integration --api-id <api-id> --integration-type AWS_PROXY --integration-uri arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:<account-id>:function:510-m3-nfl-predict-api --payload-format-version 2.0 --region us-east-1

aws apigatewayv2 create-route --api-id <api-id> --route-key 'POST /predict' --target integrations/<integration-id> --region us-east-1

aws apigatewayv2 create-route --api-id <api-id> --route-key 'GET /health' --target integrations/<integration-id> --region us-east-1

aws apigatewayv2 create-stage --api-id <api-id> --stage-name '$default' --auto-deploy --region us-east-1
  1. Let this API invoke the function, and nothing broader. The statement id is 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api.
aws lambda add-permission --function-name 510-m3-nfl-predict-api --statement-id 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal apigateway.amazonaws.com --source-arn arn:aws:execute-api:us-east-1:<account-id>:<api-id>/*/* --region us-east-1
  1. Set CORS. Write the file, then apply it. The only origin is http://localhost:5173.
cat > build/cors.json <<'EOF'
{
  "AllowOrigins": ["http://localhost:5173"],
  "AllowMethods": ["POST", "GET", "OPTIONS"],
  "AllowHeaders": ["content-type"],
  "MaxAge": 300
}
EOF

aws apigatewayv2 update-api --api-id <api-id> --cors-configuration file://build/cors.json --region us-east-1
  1. Tag the log group Lambda created.
aws logs tag-resource --resource-arn arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:<account-id>:log-group:/aws/lambda/510-m3-nfl-predict-api --tags project=510-m3 --region us-east-1
  1. Keep the function's logs for 14 days.
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/lambda/510-m3-nfl-predict-api --retention-in-days 14 --region us-east-1
  1. Check the public address https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/health

curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict

curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"win_pct_differential": 1.5}' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict

curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code} time %{time_total}\n' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/health

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code} time %{time_total}\n' https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/health

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -X OPTIONS https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -X OPTIONS https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict -H 'Origin: http://example.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'

docs.title: Check the Deployed Model Against the Local Model
docs.text:
These checks confirm the function is running the zip built here, and that every game gets the same answer as the local model. The expected hash of the zip is IU5bJH9pTL+rF/uEXMUAp+Eo/mik2abfaSasBXPOgbk=, and the zip is 63,452,500 bytes. Both copies of the model hash to 8fff766505a925218eae2484ae56a8ba7baed06b62ce3413ea33c8eb15e8ea4b. docs.title: Phase 4 Implementation: AWS Deployment
docs.text:
This page explains how the Phase 4 deployment works, one step at a time, with the real results. It also holds the measurement made before anything was built: the size of the Lambda package (Step 3). For the short version, see the Brief. The commands, in order, are on Deployment Guide.

Status: built and tested. The Lambda entry point is src/api/lambda_handler.py, and its tests are in tests/test_lambda_handler.py. Every number below comes from the real deployment. The full test suite passes with 53 tests (the 47 from earlier phases and 6 new ones) and no warnings. The public address is https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.

docs.title: What Is Mangum?
docs.text:
Mangum is a small Python library that lets a FastAPI app run inside AWS Lambda. It translates between two formats, and it does nothing else.

  • A normal web server (uvicorn on a laptop, see the Glossary) listens on a port and receives HTTP requests.
  • Lambda has no port. It runs a function once per request. The function receives a dictionary (called an event) and returns a dictionary.
  • API Gateway is what receives the browser's HTTP request, builds the event, and calls the Lambda function. This happens with or without Mangum.
  • Mangum runs inside the function. It turns the event into a request that FastAPI understands, calls the app, and turns FastAPI's answer back into the dictionary Lambda returns.
  • In code, the wrapper is one call, Mangum(app, lifespan="off"). See Step 1 for why the start-up step is turned off.
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant M as Mangum
    participant F as FastAPI app
    participant P as Saved model
    B->>G: POST /predict (JSON)
    G->>M: Lambda event (dictionary)
    M->>F: HTTP-style request
    F->>F: check the input
    F->>P: predict with the two inputs
    P->>F: probability
    F->>M: JSON answer
    M->>G: Lambda response (dictionary)
    G->>B: HTTP response (JSON)

The two setups run the same app. Only the front part changes:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Local["On a laptop (Phase 3)"]
        direction LR
        L1["curl"] --> L2["uvicorn"] --> L3["FastAPI app"]
    end
    subgraph Cloud["On AWS (Phase 4)"]
        direction LR
        C1["Browser"] --> C2["API Gateway"] --> C3["Lambda function"] --> C4["Mangum"] --> C5["FastAPI app<br/>(same code)"]
    end
  • Why this and not a separate Lambda function: a hand-written function would repeat the input checks and the model call in a second place, and the local tests would not cover it. See Decisions.
  • What Mangum does not do: it does not deliver requests to Lambda, set permissions, or make the public address. API Gateway and AWS permissions do those.

docs.text:
One Lambda function and one API Gateway HTTP API, both in us-east-1. Every new name follows the pattern of the existing data bucket, 510-m3-nfl-dataset: all lowercase, words joined by hyphens, starting 510-m3-nfl-, then what the thing is.

Resource Name Lambda function 510-m3-nfl-predict-api Function role 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role API Gateway HTTP API 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api (id 9awodatqc5) Staged zip (a temporary key in the existing bucket, deleted once the function was created) deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip Local zip file (not committed) build/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip

Each AWS resource that supports tags is tagged project=510-m3. The public address is https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.

What the function role is for. Lambda runs a function as an identity, and it requires one. The role 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role is that identity. It has a single permission, writing the function's own logs, and nothing else. It is not an access key and it has no access to the data bucket.

docs.title: Step 1: Add the Lambda Entry Point
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Wrap the Phase 3 app so that AWS Lambda can call it.

Why: Lambda hands a function a dictionary (an event), and FastAPI expects a web request. Mangum translates between them. See What Is Mangum?.

If skipped: There would be nothing for the function to run.

The whole file is short. These are its two functions:

def build_handler(app, config):
    """Load the saved model once and wrap the API so Lambda can call it."""
    app.state.model = load_model(config)
    return Mangum(app, lifespan="off")


def handler(event, context):
    """Build the wrapped handler on the first call, then reuse it for later calls."""
    global _cached_handler
    if _cached_handler is None:
        _cached_handler = build_handler(app, load_config())
    return _cached_handler(event, context)
  • One file, src/api/lambda_handler.py. The handler setting of the function is src.api.lambda_handler.handler.
  • build_handler loads the model with load_model from src/api/app.py, stores it on the app, and returns the app wrapped by Mangum with lifespan="off".
  • handler is the function Lambda calls. On the first call it builds the wrapped handler and keeps it in _cached_handler, so every later call reuses it. The model is therefore loaded once, on the first call.
  • Why lifespan="off". In Mangum 0.22.0 (checked in its adapter.py), when lifespan is "auto" or "on", the app's start-up step runs at the start of every invocation. That would re-read the saved model on every request. Turning it off and loading the model once in build_handler avoids that.
  • Why handler is a function and not a ready-made object. The model is read on the first call and not when the file is imported, so the file imports cleanly on a machine with no saved model, such as a test run.
  • No pandas. The file imports only mangum, src.api.app, and src.config.

docs.title: Step 2: Test the Entry Point With No AWS
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Prove the entry point answers a Lambda event correctly before anything is built or deployed.

Why: A mistake found here costs seconds. The same mistake found on AWS costs a build, an upload, and a log search.

If skipped: The first test of the wiring would be on AWS.

The tests call the entry point with a made-up event in the shape API Gateway sends for an HTTP API (payload format version 2.0). A made-up model in a temporary folder stands in for the real one, except in the last test.

# Test What it checks 1 test_handler_serves_a_predict_event A POST /predict event returns statusCode 200 and the four response fields, with the made-up model's version. 2 test_handler_serves_a_health_event A GET /health event returns 200 and status ok. 3 test_handler_rejects_a_bad_body A body with only win_pct_differential of 1.5 returns 422 and names both fields. 4 test_model_is_loaded_once_across_invocations Three calls to handler read the model once. 5 test_lambda_handler_does_not_import_pandas The file's imports are read as text, and none is pandas, mlflow, matplotlib, or from src/model/. 6 test_real_handler_worked_example With the real model (skipped if models/model.joblib is missing), the inputs -0.5 and -18.0 return 0.3296.
  • Result: 53 tests pass (47 from earlier phases and 6 new). Without models/model.joblib, 51 pass and 2 are skipped.
  • One warning is hidden. Mangum's adapter asks asyncio for the current event loop in a way Python 3.12 and later deprecate, which printed a DeprecationWarning from inside Mangum. pytest.ini hides that one warning, as it already does for one MLflow warning. Every other warning is still shown, and the run now has none.

docs.title: Step 3: Measure the Package Size
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Measure the unzipped and zipped size of the Lambda package before building the function.

Why: scikit-learn brings in scipy and numpy, which are large, and Lambda rejects a zip over its size limit. A late surprise would force a container image, ECR, and Docker into the middle of the AWS work.

If skipped: The first upload could fail with a size error after the function code, the gateway, and the permissions were already set up around it.

Status: measured. The measurement was made on a Mac by downloading the Linux packages for Lambda. Nothing was run on AWS. Sizes in this step use 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.

Answer: it fits, if the API does not install pandas. Without pandas the unzipped package is 231.3 MB, which is 30.8 MB under the limit. With pandas it is 278.4 MB, which is 16.3 MB over.

docs.title: What Limits Apply?
docs.text:
Limit Value What it means here Unzipped package, including layers 250 MB (262,144,000 bytes) The hard limit for a zip deployment. The measurement below is compared with this. Zip uploaded directly in the AWS console About 50 MB A zip over this is uploaded through S3 or the AWS command-line tool instead. Container image 10 GB The fall-back if the zip does not fit.

Sources: AWS Lambda layers documentation for the 250 MB limit, and an AWS re:Post answer for the byte count. The 50 MB console limit is approximate. The limits can change, so check the current AWS page before relying on the numbers.

docs.title: How Was the Size Measured?
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Install the serving packages<br/>as Linux arm64, Python 3.13"] --> B["Remove __pycache__ folders"]
    B --> C["Copy in src/, config/,<br/>and models/model.joblib"]
    C --> D["Add up the bytes of every file"]
    C --> E["Zip the folder and<br/>check the zip size"]

The packages were installed into a build folder with a command that picks the Lambda platform instead of the Mac's:

pip install --target build/lambda --implementation cp --python-version 3.13 --platform manylinux_2_28_aarch64 --platform manylinux2014_aarch64 --only-binary=:all: --no-compile scikit-learn==1.9.1 numpy==2.5.4 joblib==1.6.0 PyYAML==6.0.3 fastapi==0.162.2 pydantic==2.14.3 mangum==0.22.0
Part of the command What it does --platform manylinux_2_28_aarch64 and manylinux2014_aarch64 Download packages built for Linux on an arm64 chip, which is what the Lambda function will use. --python-version 3.13 and --implementation cp Match the Python 3.13 runtime. --only-binary=:all: Use ready-built packages only. Nothing is compiled on the Mac, which could not produce Linux files. --no-compile Skip the cached .pyc files, which the zip does not need.
  • Included: scikit-learn, numpy, joblib, PyYAML, fastapi, pydantic, mangum, and the packages they pull in (among them scipy and narwhals). scipy resolved to 1.18.1.
  • Project files added: src/, config/, and models/model.joblib.
  • Left out: mlflow, matplotlib, boto3, pytest, and uvicorn. Lambda does not run a web server, so uvicorn is not needed there, and Lambda already provides boto3.
  • Measured twice: once without pandas and once with it, because pandas is large.

docs.title: What Did the Measurement Show?
docs.text:
Package set Unzipped Zipped Against the 250 MB limit Without pandas 231.3 MB 63.2 MB 30.8 MB under With pandas 278.4 MB 75.1 MB 16.3 MB over

The largest folders in the package without pandas:

Folder Size What it holds scipy 89.4 MB Math routines that scikit-learn depends on sklearn 39.4 MB scikit-learn itself scipy.libs 31.8 MB Compiled libraries bundled with scipy numpy.libs 28.7 MB Compiled libraries bundled with numpy numpy 25.4 MB numpy itself pydantic_core 4.8 MB The compiled core of pydantic yaml 2.9 MB PyYAML narwhals 2.1 MB A small helper package that scikit-learn depends on
  • pandas alone adds 46.0 MB, which is what pushes the package over the limit.
  • The zipped file is 63.2 MB, which is over the console's direct-upload limit of about 50 MB. Upload it through S3 or the AWS command-line tool.
  • Result for the plan: the zip route works, so ECR and a container image are not needed for Lambda. The fall-back stays unused unless the package grows past the limit.

docs.title: What Does This Mean for the Phase 3 API?
docs.text:
The API must run without pandas. Three facts about the current code shape this:

  • src/model/features.py imports pandas at the top. Any API file that imports from it (for example to reuse INPUT_COLUMNS) would pull pandas into the package. The saved model file already holds the input names (feature_names), so the API reads them from there instead.
  • The model works without pandas. In a fresh environment with only scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy, joblib, scipy, and PyYAML, the saved model loaded, and the inputs -0.5 and -18.0 passed in as a plain numpy array gave a home win probability of 0.3296, the same as the worked example in Part 2. pandas was not imported at any point.
  • One warning is expected. The scaler was fitted on a table with column names, so a plain array makes scikit-learn print "X does not have valid feature names". The probability is the same. The API silences this one warning.

These points are recorded in the Phase 3 Brief.

docs.title: What Was Not Known at the Time?
docs.text:
• Whether it runs on AWS. The packages were downloaded for Linux but not run there when this was measured. Steps 6, 9, and 10 are the proof, and the function ran with no import error.
  • Unpinned scipy. requirements.txt does not pin scipy, which scikit-learn brings in. The serving list in Step 4 pins it at 1.18.1, the version measured here.
  • Growth. The function code adds almost nothing, but a version bump of any large package changes the total. Re-measure after changing a pin.
  • Margin. The built zip is 231,252,596 bytes unzipped, about 30.9 MB (12% of the limit) under 262,144,000 bytes. That leaves room for small additions and not for pandas.

docs.title: How Is the Measurement Repeated?
docs.text:
Run the install command above from the project folder, then remove the cached files:

find build/lambda -name __pycache__ -type d -exec rm -rf {} +

Copy in src/, config/, and models/model.joblib, then count the bytes:

find build/lambda -type f -exec cat {} + | wc -c

build/ is already in .gitignore. Compare the result with 262,144,000.

docs.title: Step 4: Build the Zip
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Produce build/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip with exactly what the function needs.

Why: The function runs only what is in the zip, on Linux, so the zip must be built for that platform and hold the project files in the layout the code expects.

If skipped: There would be nothing to upload.

  • A short pinned list, requirements-serve.txt. It names scikit-learn==1.9.1, numpy==2.5.4, scipy==1.18.1, joblib==1.6.0, PyYAML==6.0.3, fastapi==0.162.2, pydantic==2.14.3, and mangum==0.22.0. It leaves out pandas, mlflow, matplotlib, boto3 (Lambda provides it), uvicorn (Mangum replaces it), and the test packages.
  • Install for the function's platform, with the command from Step 3, reading the list with -r requirements-serve.txt.
  • Project files, in the project's folder layout: src/config.py, src/api/app.py, src/api/lambda_handler.py, src/api/schemas.py, config/config.yaml, and models/model.joblib. The folders src/data/ and src/model/ are left out, because the function does not use them and src/model/ imports pandas. resolve_path finds the project folder from the code's own location, so the same paths work in the zip.
  • Zip the contents, so src/, config/, and models/ sit at the top of the zip.
  • The built zip:
    • 125 compiled libraries under numpy/ and scipy/, every one for aarch64, and none for darwin or x86_64.
    • 231,252,596 bytes unzipped and 63,452,500 bytes zipped, matching the Step 3 measurement.
    • It holds no pandas, mlflow, or src/model, and scipy-1.18.1 matches the pin.
  • The saved model must match the zip. The model file was saved by scikit-learn 1.9.1, and the zip holds the same version, or the service refuses to start, as in Phase 3.

docs.title: Step 5: Create the Role and the Function
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Create the Lambda function with permission to do one thing: write its own logs.

Why: The function needs no other AWS access. Each identity gets only the access its job needs.

If skipped: There would be no function for the gateway to call.

  • The role 510-m3-nfl-predict-api-role can be assumed only by Lambda, and has one policy attached, the AWS managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole, which only writes logs. Its trust policy has no statement id, because IAM rejected a hyphenated one with MalformedPolicyDocument.
  • The zip is staged in S3. At 63.2 MB it is over the console's direct-upload limit, so it was copied to deploy/510-m3-nfl-predict-api.zip in the data bucket, the function was created from it, and the staged copy was deleted. The bucket holds no deploy/ object now.
  • Function settings:
Setting Value Runtime python3.13 Architecture arm64 Handler src.api.lambda_handler.handler Memory 1769 MB Timeout 10 seconds Environment variable JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING = 0 (the only one) VPC, layers, reserved concurrency none
  • The environment variable. The function's first log printed "joblib will operate in serial mode", because Lambda has no multiprocessing directory. Setting JOBLIB_MULTIPROCESSING=0 makes joblib skip that check. The function never uses multiprocessing, and the line is gone from every later log.
  • Log retention. The log group /aws/lambda/510-m3-nfl-predict-api keeps logs for 14 days, and is tagged project=510-m3.

docs.title: What Is the Memory Setting?
docs.text: Lambda gives a function CPU in proportion to its memory. The function runs at 1769 MB. Accuracy is the only priority for this deployment. Latency and cost are not concerns, so the memory may be changed if that helps, but it is not a priority. See Decisions.

docs.title: Step 6: Test the Function in AWS
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Invoke the function directly, with no gateway, and read its logs.

Why: This is the first time the Linux packages run, and a problem here is easier to read than one that comes back through the gateway.

If skipped: A package that fails to import on Lambda would show up later as a plain gateway error.

  • Three invocations, using the same made-up events as Step 2: the worked example, the health check, and a bad body.
  • Results:
    • The worked example returned status 200 and {"prediction": 0, "predicted_label": "away win", "home_win_probability": 0.3296, "model_version": "v1.0"}.
    • The health check returned 200 and the expected health body.
    • The bad body returned 422, naming both fields.
    • The logs showed no start-up refusal and no import error.

docs.title: Step 7: Create the API Gateway HTTP API
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Give the function a public HTTPS address with exactly two routes.

Why: Lambda has no public address of its own. API Gateway receives the browser's request and calls the function.

If skipped: The function could be invoked only with AWS credentials.

  • An HTTP API named 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api (id 9awodatqc5) with a Lambda proxy integration (AWS_PROXY, payload format version 2.0).
  • Two routes only: POST /predict and GET /health, with no authorizer and no catch-all route.
  • The $default stage with automatic deployment.
  • Permission to call the function is given to this one API and nothing broader: the source is this API's ARN, arn:aws:execute-api:us-east-1:<account-id>:9awodatqc5/*/*. The permission's statement id is 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api.
  • The invoke URL is https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
  • No protection rules, request limit, or firewall for now. The API is public, with no key.

docs.title: Step 8: Set CORS on the Gateway
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Let the browser web app call /predict from its own address.

Why: A browser refuses a response from another address unless that address is allowed. CORS is set on the gateway only, not in the FastAPI app.

If skipped: The web app would work in curl and fail in the browser.

  • Allowed origin: http://localhost:5173, the default address of the Vite development server, and nothing else. The CloudFront address is added in Phase 5 once it exists.
  • Allowed methods: POST, GET, and OPTIONS. Allowed headers: content-type. Max age: 300 seconds.
  • Checks:
    • A preflight request from http://localhost:5173 returned status 204 with access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173.
    • The same preflight from http://example.com returned 204 with no access-control-allow-origin header, so that origin is not allowed.

docs.title: Step 9: Check the Public Address
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Confirm the deployed API answers real requests from the internet, with the same results as the local one.

Why: This is the test that matters. Everything before it checked a part.

If skipped: The phase would end with an API nobody has called.

curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/health

{"status":"ok","model_version":"v1.0","scikit_learn_version":"1.9.1"}
HTTP 200

curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"win_pct_differential": -0.5, "point_diff_per_game_differential": -18.0}' https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/predict

{"prediction":0,"predicted_label":"away win","home_win_probability":0.3296,"model_version":"v1.0"}
HTTP 200
Request Result GET /health 200, the health body above POST /predict with -0.5 and -18.0 200, home win probability 0.3296, prediction 0 POST /predict with only win_pct_differential of 1.5 422, naming both fields GET /predict 404, {"message":"Not Found"}, because the gateway has no route for it

docs.title: Step 10: Check the Deployed Model Against the Local Model
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Prove the model on AWS gives the same answers as the local model, on every game.

Why: Accuracy is the only priority. The packages on Lambda are Linux builds, so the arithmetic could in principle differ from the Mac that trained the model.

If skipped: The deployed model could be slightly different and nobody would know.

First, is the function running what was built here?

  • The zip: the base64 SHA-256 hash of the local zip equals the CodeSha256 that Lambda stores for the function (IU5bJH9pTL+rF/uEXMUAp+Eo/mik2abfaSasBXPOgbk=).
  • The model file: the SHA-256 of models/model.joblib and of the copy inside the zip are both 8fff766505a925218eae2484ae56a8ba7baed06b62ce3413ea33c8eb15e8ea4b.
  • The data: the SHA-256 of data/from-s3/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv equals data_sha256 in results/run-summary.json (7219e8a8672b900af9facbb54d8a28f9f2a34df9ede3b8385a735768082517fb).

Then, every game through the public API. A local script (build/parity_check.py, kept on the developer's machine and not committed) builds the local answers with the saved model, and sends each of the 1,759 games to POST /predict, one at a time, then compares each answer.

Result Value Requests sent 1,759 (1,339 training, 271 validation, 149 test) Retries 0 Status 200 answers 1,759 Picks that match the local pick 1,759 Probabilities that match the local probability (rounded to 4 places) 1,759, with a largest difference of 0.0 Slowest and average request 0.29 s and 0.033 s Group Correct from the deployed answers Committed run summary Training 820 of 1,339 820 of 1,339 Validation 171 of 271 171 of 271 Test 88 of 149 88 of 149

The deployed model and the local model are the same at the 4-decimal precision the API returns, and the accuracy from the deployed answers equals the accuracy in the run summary. This does not test the browser, CORS from a real front end, or behavior under load.

docs.title: Step 11: Write the Steps Down
docs.text:
Purpose

Goal: Make the deployment repeatable by hand.

Why: Written steps mean the deployment does not depend on anyone's memory, and they show exactly what was created, so it can be removed again.

If skipped: Nobody could rebuild or remove the deployment without redoing the work from scratch.

  • Deployment Guide lists every command of Steps 4 to 10, in order, with placeholders such as <account-id> and <api-id> for values that differ between accounts. It ends with the commands that remove everything this phase created. Those removal commands are written, and not run.
  • No deploy.yml workflow. The steps are run by hand. See Decisions.

docs.title: What Is Left to Watch?
docs.text:
• The zip has about 30.9 MB of room. A new large dependency, or a version bump, can push it over. Re-measure after changing a pin.
  • The API has no protection rules, request limit, or firewall. Anyone can call it. That is acceptable for this project.
  • CORS allows only the local web app. The CloudFront address is added in Phase 5.

The Brief lists the original risks.

docs.title: From Data to Decisions: Deploying a Reproducible ML Pipeline
docs.text: This project is an opportunity to design, build, and deploy a full-stack machine learning system. You and your partner will select a dataset, host it in a cloud storage or database system, and build a reproducible pipeline that trains and tracks a simple ML model. You'll then containerize and deploy your model as an API endpoint on a cloud platform and create a front-end application that consumes this API. The project emphasizes best practices in MLOps, including reproducibility, cloud deployment, and modular design.

docs.title: Learning Goals
docs.text:
• Practice sourcing, cleaning, and hosting real-world data in the cloud
  • Build reproducible, modular ML pipelines using configuration files and containers
  • Track experiments using MLFlow or Weights & Biases
  • Deploy a model as an API endpoint using cloud services
  • Build a lightweight front-end to consume a live model API
  • Follow GitHub best practices for collaboration and version control
  • Reflect on ethical implications and limitations of your ML application

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: Your final deliverables consist of a GitHub repository and a link to a deployed front-end application.

docs.title: 1. GitHub Repository
docs.text:
Your repository must include:

  • All code for preprocessing, training, serving, and deployment
  • config.yaml for pipeline configuration
  • requirements.txt or environment.yaml
  • A Dockerfile that can run the full project
  • Clear documentation for:
    • How to train the model
    • How to build and test the API locally
    • How to deploy to the cloud
  • MLFlow or Weights & Biases logging
  • Use of branches and pull requests (each group member must submit at least one PR)
  • A clear project structure and commit history

docs.title: 2. Front-End Application
docs.text:
Your app must:

  • Be publicly accessible and linked in the README
  • Send requests to your deployed model API (e.g., using requests or fetch)
  • Display the model's predictions in an interactive, intuitive format
  • Be built with Streamlit, Gradio, NextJS, or a custom web framework

docs.title: 1. Choose a Dataset and Define the Problem
docs.text:
• Select a public dataset (e.g., Kaggle, UCI, HuggingFace Datasets).
  • Define a supervised learning task (classification or regression).
  • Identify your target variable and evaluation metric.

docs.title: 2. Set Up Data Storage in the Cloud
docs.text:
• Clean and preprocess the dataset locally.
  • Upload your cleaned data to a cloud storage service:
    • Google Cloud Storage (GCS)
    • AWS S3
    • Firebase Storage
    • Cloud-hosted PostgreSQL (e.g., via Google Cloud SQL or Supabase)
  • Write a script to access and download the data programmatically in your pipeline.

docs.title: 3. Build a Reproducible ML Pipeline
docs.text:
• Choose a simple model (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost).
  • Implement a pipeline that includes:
    • Data ingestion (from the cloud)
    • Preprocessing and feature engineering
    • Train/validation/test split
    • Model training and evaluation
  • Control parameters via a config.yaml file (e.g., learning rate, split ratio, etc.).

NOTE: We are not assessing your ML model. Your model could have terrible accuracy. That is fine! Not the point of the assignment, don't get hung up on your model.

docs.title: 4. Track Experiments
docs.text:
Use MLFlow or Weights & Biases to:

  • Track experiment runs, model parameters, and evaluation metrics.
  • Log artifacts (trained model, plots, etc.) for version control and reproducibility.

docs.title: 5. Containerize with Docker
docs.text:
Create a Dockerfile that:

  • Installs all dependencies.
  • Includes entry points for training and serving.

Build and run your Docker image locally to test reproducibility.

docs.title: 6. Serve Your Model as an API
docs.text:
Use FastAPI or Flask to:

  • Load your trained model.
  • Create a /predict endpoint that accepts JSON input and returns a prediction.
  • Test your API locally using curl or Postman.

docs.title: 7. Deploy the API to the Cloud
docs.text:
Choose a cloud deployment platform:

  • Google Cloud Run or Cloud Functions
  • AWS Lambda with API Gateway
  • Azure Functions

Package your API and deploy it so that the /predict endpoint is publicly accessible. Confirm your endpoint works using an HTTP request with test data.

docs.title: 8. Build the Front-End Interface
docs.text:
• Create a lightweight UI using Streamlit, Gradio, or a simple web app.
  • Collect user input, send it to the deployed API using requests or fetch, and display the prediction.
  • Host your app on Hugging Face Spaces, Streamlit Cloud, Vercel [all free!], or a custom deployment platform.
  • Include the link to the live front-end in your README.

docs.title: 9. Document Everything and Follow Best Practices
docs.text:
Your GitHub README must include:

  • Project overview and goals
  • Dataset description and link
  • Model architecture and evaluation
  • Cloud services used
  • Setup and usage instructions
  • Link to deployed API and front-end app

docs.title: Project Requirements
docs.text:
End-to-end requirements for one person building this project, stated as checkable items. The full assignment brief is in the Project Instructions.

Two things are delivered: a GitHub repository with the full pipeline, and a publicly reachable front-end linked from the repository README.

docs.title: 1. Problem and Dataset
docs.text:
• Pick a public dataset (for example from Kaggle, UCI, or Hugging Face Datasets).
  • Define a single supervised learning task: either classification or regression.
  • Name the target variable and the one evaluation metric used to judge the model.

docs.title: 2. Cloud Data Storage
docs.text:
• Clean and preprocess the dataset locally before uploading.
  • Upload the cleaned data to an Amazon S3 bucket. S3 is the chosen storage service for this project.
  • Include a script that downloads the data from S3 programmatically (for example with boto3), so the pipeline starts from the S3 copy rather than a local file.

docs.title: 3. Reproducible Pipeline
docs.text:
• Use one simple model (for example logistic regression, random forest, or XGBoost).
  • The pipeline must cover, in order: data ingestion from S3, preprocessing and feature engineering, a train/validation/test split, model training, and evaluation.
  • All tunable settings live in a config.yaml file (for example the split ratio and model parameters). Changing a run means editing that file, not the code.
  • Model accuracy is not graded. A poor score is acceptable; the requirement is a clean, repeatable process.

docs.title: 4. Experiment Tracking
docs.text:
• Use MLflow or Weights & Biases.
  • Log each run's parameters and evaluation metrics.
  • Log artifacts for reproducibility: at minimum the trained model, plus any plots produced.

docs.title: 5. Docker
docs.text:
• Provide a Dockerfile that installs every dependency and defines entry points for both training and serving.
  • The image must build and run locally so the project is reproducible from the container alone.

docs.title: 6. Prediction API
docs.text:
• Serve the trained model with FastAPI or Flask.
  • Expose a /predict endpoint that accepts JSON input and returns a prediction as JSON.
  • The endpoint must be testable locally (for example with curl or Postman).

docs.title: 7. Cloud Deployment
docs.text:
• Deploy the API on AWS. AWS is the chosen deployment platform for this project; use AWS Lambda fronted by API Gateway.
  • Configure CORS on API Gateway so the browser-based front-end can call /predict.
  • After deployment, the /predict endpoint must be publicly reachable and must return a valid response to an HTTP request with test data.

docs.title: 8. Front-End
docs.text:
• Build a lightweight interface with Vite. Use the Vite development server for local work and vite build to produce the files that are published.
  • The interface collects user input, sends it to the deployed API, and displays the returned prediction in an interactive, readable form.
  • Host the built files on AWS: a private S3 bucket served over HTTPS through a CloudFront distribution. CloudFront is the chosen hosting platform for this project.
  • Link the live front-end URL in the repository README.

docs.title: 9. Repository Contents
docs.text:
The GitHub repository must contain all of the following:

  • Code for preprocessing, training, serving, and deployment.
  • config.yaml for pipeline configuration.
  • A dependency file: requirements.txt or environment.yaml.
  • A Dockerfile that runs the full project.
  • MLflow or Weights & Biases logging wired into the pipeline.
  • A clear project structure and a readable commit history.
  • Work done on branches merged through pull requests, with at least one pull request on record.

docs.title: 10. README
docs.text:
The repository README must include:

  • A project overview and its goals.
  • A description of the dataset and a link to it.
  • The model used and its evaluation result.
  • The cloud services used.
  • Setup and usage instructions covering how to train the model, how to build and test the API locally, and how to deploy to the cloud.
  • Links to both the deployed API and the live front-end.

docs.title: Acceptance Checklist
docs.text: # Requirement Done when 1 Problem and dataset Public dataset chosen; task, target, and metric named. 2 Cloud storage Cleaned data uploaded to Amazon S3; download script pulls it from the bucket. 3 Pipeline Ingestion → preprocessing → split → train → evaluate, all driven by config.yaml. 4 Tracking Runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts logged to MLflow or W&B. 5 Docker Image builds and runs locally with training and serving entry points. 6 API /predict returns a prediction from JSON input, verified locally. 7 Deployment API runs on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway; /predict is publicly reachable, answers test requests, and allows the front-end's origin through CORS. 8 Front-end Vite app served from S3 through CloudFront calls the live API and shows predictions. 9 Repository All required files present; branch-and-PR workflow with at least one PR. 10 README Overview, dataset, model, cloud services, setup/usage, and both live links.

docs.title: Requirements Map
docs.text: This page maps each requirement that is done so far to where it lives in the repository. Each entry gives the requirement as written in Project Requirements, then the file, the function, the setting, or the command that covers it, and the docs page that explains it. A new entry is added when a phase finishes.

docs.title: 1. Problem and Dataset
docs.text:
• Pick a public dataset (for example from Kaggle, UCI, or Hugging Face Datasets).
    • What: the nflverse games.csv file, one row per NFL game since 1999.
    • Where: the address is data.source_url in config/config.yaml. src/data/fetch_raw.py downloads it and saves it as data/raw/games.csv.
    • Docs: What Is the Source Data?
  • Define a single supervised learning task: either classification or regression.
    • What: binary classification. Did the home team win?
    • Where: the answer is the home_win column built in build_model_table in src/model/features.py.
    • Docs: What Is the Prediction Task?
  • Name the target variable and the one evaluation metric used to judge the model.
    • Target: home_win (1 if the home team won, 0 if not), listed in MODEL_COLUMNS in src/model/features.py.
    • Metric: accuracy, next to the always-pick-home baseline. It is computed by score_group in src/model/evaluate.py. Log loss is a second score that checks the win percentages.
    • Docs: What Is Accuracy?

docs.title: 2. Cloud Data Storage
docs.text:
• Clean and preprocess the dataset locally before uploading.
    • Where: clean_games in src/data/clean.py, run with python -m src.data.clean. It writes data/processed/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv.
    • Docs: Step 2: Clean the Raw Data
  • Upload the cleaned data to an Amazon S3 bucket. S3 is the chosen storage service for this project.
    • Where: upload in src/data/upload_to_s3.py, run with python -m src.data.upload_to_s3. The bucket name and file name are data.s3_bucket and data.s3_key in config/config.yaml.
    • The bucket itself: 510-m3-nfl-dataset in us-east-1. It was created by hand in the AWS console, so no file in the repository creates it.
    • Docs: Step 3: Upload the Cleaned Table to S3
  • Include a script that downloads the data from S3 programmatically (for example with boto3), so the pipeline starts from the S3 copy rather than a local file.
    • Where: download in src/data/download_from_s3.py, run with python -m src.data.download_from_s3. It saves data/from-s3/nfl_matchups_2020_2026.csv.
    • Starting from the S3 copy: load_games in src/model/features.py reads only that downloaded file, never the local cleaned table.
    • Docs: Step 4: Download the Cleaned Table From S3

docs.title: 3. Reproducible Pipeline
docs.text:
• Use one simple model (for example logistic regression, random forest, or XGBoost).
    • What: logistic regression behind a standardizing step, kept together as one pipeline.
    • Where: build_pipeline and fit_pipeline in src/model/train.py.
    • Docs: Step 4: Fit the Scaler and the Model
  • The pipeline must cover, in order: data ingestion from S3, preprocessing and feature engineering, a train/validation/test split, model training, and evaluation.
    • Ingestion from S3: src/data/download_from_s3.py, then load_games in src/model/features.py.
    • Preprocessing: src/data/clean.py.
    • Feature engineering: standings_before_week and build_model_table in src/model/features.py. Docs: Step 1: Feature Engineering.
    • Train/validation/test split: split_games in src/model/features.py, with split_seasons in src/config.py. Docs: Step 2: Split the Games by Season.
    • Model training: fit_pipeline in src/model/train.py.
    • Evaluation: score_group and plot_confusion_matrix in src/model/evaluate.py. Docs: Step 5: Score the Model.
    • How they run: the data steps are separate commands (fetch, clean, upload, download). python -m src.model.train then runs the rest in order: load the downloaded table, build the inputs, split, fit, score, save, and log.
  • All tunable settings live in a config.yaml file (for example the split ratio and model parameters). Changing a run means editing that file, not the code.
    • Where: config/config.yaml, read through src/config.py. Its blocks are data (paths, bucket, region), window (first and last season, and the last scored week), split (last training season and the validation season), model (version, seed, output file, and the logistic regression settings), and tracking (MLflow names and folders).
    • Two things live in code, not in the file: the 0.5 cutoff that turns a probability into a pick, and the list of columns that cleaning keeps.
    • Docs: Step 3: Add the Model and Tracking Settings
  • Model accuracy is not graded. A poor score is acceptable; the requirement is a clean, repeatable process.
    • Where: two runs with the same settings give identical scores. test_same_settings_give_the_same_probabilities in tests/test_train.py checks it, and results/run-summary.json is byte for byte the same on every run with the same settings and data.

docs.title: 4. Experiment Tracking
docs.text:
• Use MLflow or Weights & Biases.
    • What: MLflow. Its settings are the tracking block in config/config.yaml.
    • Where: log_run in src/model/train.py.
  • Log each run's parameters and evaluation metrics.
    • Parameters (15): model_version, random_seed, C, solver, max_iter, feature_names, train_start_season, train_end_season, validation_season, test_season, n_train, n_validation, n_test, scikit_learn_version, and data_sha256 (a fingerprint of the downloaded table, from file_fingerprint in src/model/train.py).
    • Metrics (8): train_accuracy, validation_accuracy, test_accuracy, validation_log_loss, test_log_loss, baseline_train, baseline_validation, baseline_test.
    • Automatic tags: MLflow also records the git commit, branch, and repository address of each run.
    • Docs: What Is Logged for Each Run?
  • Log artifacts for reproducibility: at minimum the trained model, plus any plots produced.
    • Files stored with each run (3): model/model.joblib (the trained model), plots/confusion_matrix_validation.png (the one plot), and config/config.yaml (a copy of the settings used).
    • The plot is drawn by plot_confusion_matrix in src/model/evaluate.py.
    • A second copy of the model, in MLflow's own format: each run also has one logged model, pipeline-mlflow-format, stored under mlartifacts/models/. model/model.joblib stays the working copy that the API will load.
    • A readable record outside MLflow: results/run-summary.json, written by write_run_summary in src/model/train.py. It holds the settings, the data fingerprint, the scores, and the learned weights, and it is committed to git.
  • Where to find the recorded runs:
    • In the repository: results/run-summary.json shows the latest run's settings, scores, and learned weights without MLflow.
    • Run record: mlflow.db in the project folder. Run files: mlartifacts/. Both are created by training and are not committed.
    • To browse them: run mlflow ui --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db and open the address it prints.
    • The saved model file: models/model.joblib, also not committed.

docs.title: 6. Prediction API
docs.text:
• Serve the trained model with FastAPI or Flask.
    • What: FastAPI. The app, the start-up step that loads the saved model once, and the 0.5 pick rule are in src/api/app.py (create_app, load_model, label_for).
    • Docs: How Does the Service Work?
  • Expose a /predict endpoint that accepts JSON input and returns a prediction as JSON.
    • Where: POST /predict in src/api/app.py, with the request and response shapes in src/api/schemas.py. The request holds win_pct_differential and point_diff_per_game_differential. The response holds prediction, predicted_label, home_win_probability, and model_version.
    • Docs: What Is in the Response?
  • The endpoint must be testable locally (for example with curl or Postman).
    • How: start it with python -m uvicorn src.api.app:app --port 8000, then send requests with curl or open the test page at /docs. 17 tests in tests/test_api.py cover both routes, the input checks, and the start-up checks.
    • Docs: How Do I Run It Locally?

docs.title: 7. Cloud Deployment
docs.text:
• Deploy the API on AWS; use AWS Lambda fronted by API Gateway.
    • Where: the Lambda function 510-m3-nfl-predict-api (entry point src/api/lambda_handler.py, packages listed in requirements-serve.txt) behind the HTTP API 510-m3-nfl-predict-http-api, both in us-east-1. The commands are on Deployment Guide.
    • Docs: Phase 4 Implementation
  • Configure CORS on API Gateway so the browser-based front-end can call /predict.
    • Where: set on the gateway, not in the app. It allows the origin http://localhost:5173 for now, the methods POST, GET, and OPTIONS, and the header content-type. The CloudFront address is added in Phase 5.
    • Docs: Step 8: Set CORS on the Gateway
  • After deployment, /predict must be publicly reachable and must return a valid response to an HTTP request with test data.
    • Public address: https://9awodatqc5.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. POST /predict with the inputs -0.5 and -18.0 returns {"prediction": 0, "predicted_label": "away win", "home_win_probability": 0.3296, "model_version": "v1.0"}.
    • Checked on every game: all 1,759 games sent through the public address gave the same pick and probability as the local model.
    • Docs: Step 9: Check the Public Address and Step 10

docs.title: 9. Repository Contents
docs.text:
• Code for preprocessing, training, serving, and deployment.
    • Preprocessing: src/data/ (fetch_raw.py, clean.py, upload_to_s3.py, download_from_s3.py) and src/model/features.py.
    • Training: src/model/train.py and src/model/evaluate.py.
    • Serving: src/api/app.py and src/api/schemas.py.
    • Deployment: src/api/lambda_handler.py, requirements-serve.txt, and the written commands on Deployment Guide.
  • config.yaml for pipeline configuration. config/config.yaml.
  • A dependency file: requirements.txt or environment.yaml. requirements.txt, with every package pinned to an exact version.
  • MLflow or Weights & Biases logging wired into the pipeline. log_run is called by main in src/model/train.py, so python -m src.model.train logs a run by itself.
  • A clear project structure and a readable commit history.
    • Layout: src/data/ (Phase 1 steps), src/model/ (Phase 2 code), src/api/ (Phases 3 and 4 code), results/ (the committed run summary), .github/workflows/ (the docs site publishing workflow), src/config.py (reads the settings), tests/ (one test file per code file), config/ (settings), and docs/ (these pages).
    • Tests: pytest runs all of tests/. They use made-up data and a stand-in S3 client, so they need no internet and no AWS account.
  • Work done on branches merged through pull requests, with at least one pull request on record.
    • Where: pull requests #1 (phase_one), #2 (phase-two), and #3 (phase-three) are merged into main, and show in git log and on the GitHub repository's Pull requests tab. Phase 4 is on the branch phase-four.
